terms: Recall equation

One of the 23 equations in the first Appendix A list. It is not printed on any equation sheet, so a student must write it from memory, substitute values and rearrange it when solving quantitative problems.
Standard SI unit

The unit the Appendix A equations assume: kilogram for mass, metre for length, second for time, and so on. Values given in grams, centimetres, minutes or hours are converted to SI units before substitution.
HT flag
The letters HT beside an equation in the left hand column, marking an equation that only Higher Tier papers can require. Foundation Tier papers do not ask for it.
Weight
The force acting on a mass because of a gravitational field, found from weight = mass x gravitational field strength (g), W = m g, and measured in newtons.
Work done
Energy transferred when a force moves an object along the line of action of that force, given by work done = force x distance, W = F s, measured in joules.
Spring constant
The stiffness of a spring, k in force applied to a spring = spring constant x extension, F = k e. Extension is the increase in length, not the total length.
Moment of a force
The turning effect of a force about a pivot, moment of a force = force x distance (normal to direction of force), M = F d, in newton metres.
Pressure
Force acting normally per unit area of a surface: pressure = (force normal to a surface)/(area of that surface), p = F/A, in pascals.
Speed
The rate at which distance is covered, used as distance travelled = speed x time, s = v t, with distance in metres and time in seconds.
Acceleration
The rate of change of velocity, acceleration = (change in velocity)/(time taken), a = (∆v)/(t), measured in metres per second squared.
Resultant force
The single force equivalent to all the forces on an object. Only the resultant force is used in resultant force = mass x acceleration, F = m a.
Momentum
A property of a moving object given by momentum = mass x velocity, p = m v, measured in kilogram metres per second. It is a Higher Tier recall equation.
Kinetic energy
The energy of a moving object, kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x (speed)^2, E_k = 1/2 m v^2. The speed is squared but the mass is not.
Gravitational potential energy
Energy stored by raising a mass in a gravitational field, gravitational potential energy = mass x gravitational field strength (g) x height, E_p = m g h.
Power
The rate of energy transfer, power = (energy transferred)/(time), P = E/t, measured in watts. One watt is one joule per second.
Power from work
The rate of doing work, power = (work done)/(time), P = W/t. It gives the same value as P = E/t because work done is energy transferred.
Efficiency
The fraction of the energy supplied that is usefully transferred: efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer). It has no unit and cannot exceed 1.
Efficiency from power
The same ratio expressed using power: efficiency = (useful power output)/(total power input). It is used when powers rather than energies are given.
Wave speed
The speed at which a wave transfers energy, wave speed = frequency x wavelength, v = f λ, with frequency in hertz and wavelength in metres.
Charge flow
The quantity of charge moved by a current in a time, charge flow = current x time, Q = I t, in coulombs.
Resistance
The opposition of a component to current, appearing in potential difference = current x resistance, V = I R, with resistance in ohms.
Electrical power
The rate of energy transfer in a circuit, power = potential difference x current, P = V I.
Power dissipated in a resistor
Power calculated from current and resistance alone: power = (current)^2 x resistance, P = I^2 R. The current is squared, not the resistance.
Energy transferred by an appliance
Energy found from energy transferred = power x time, E = P t, with power in watts and time in seconds.
Energy transferred by charge
Energy found from energy transferred = charge flow x potential difference, E = Q V, with charge in coulombs.
Density
Mass per unit volume, density = (mass)/(volume), ρ = m/V, in kilograms per cubic metre when SI units are used.
Equation sheet equation
One of the 12 equations printed on the Physics equation sheet. It does not have to be recalled, but the right one must be selected and applied correctly.
HT flag on the sheet
The HT marking on the equation sheet list, showing which of the printed equations only Higher Tier papers can require.
Pressure in a liquid column
Pressure due to a column of liquid = height of column x density of liquid x gravitational field strength (g), p = h ρ g. It depends on depth, not on the width of the container.
Uniform acceleration equation
(final velocity)^2 - (initial velocity)^2 = 2 x acceleration x distance, v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s, used when time is not known.
Rate of change of momentum
Force expressed as force = (change in momentum)/(time taken), F = (m ∆v)/(∆t). A longer impact time gives a smaller force for the same change in momentum.
Elastic potential energy
Energy stored in a stretched spring, elastic potential energy = 0.5 x spring constant x (extension)^2, E_e = 1/2 k e^2.
Specific heat capacity
The constant c in change in thermal energy = mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change, ∆E = m c ∆θ: the energy needed to raise one kilogram by one degree.
Period
The time for one complete wave or oscillation, period = (1)/(frequency), measured in seconds.
Magnification
A ratio found from magnification = (image height)/(object height). Because it is a ratio of two lengths it has no unit.
Magnetic flux density
The quantity B in force on a conductor (at right angles to a magnetic field) carrying a current = magnetic flux density x current x length, F = B I l, measured in tesla.
Specific latent heat
The constant L in thermal energy for a change of state = mass x specific latent heat, E = m L: the energy to change the state of one kilogram with no temperature change.
Transformer turns ratio
The relation (potential difference across primary coil)/(potential difference across secondary coil) = (number of turns in primary coil)/(number of turns in secondary coil), V_p/V_s = n_p/n_s.
Transformer power relation

For a transformer assumed to be 100% efficient, potential difference across primary coil x current in primary coil = potential difference across secondary coil x current in secondary coil, V_p I_p = V_s I_s.
Constant for a gas
For gases: pressure x volume = constant, p V = constant, at constant temperature for a fixed mass of gas.
Eukaryotic cell
A cell that has its genetic material enclosed in a nucleus. Plant and animal cells are eukaryotic cells; they also have a cell membrane and cytoplasm.
Prokaryotic cell

A cell whose genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus. Bacterial cells are prokaryotic cells: they have cytoplasm and a cell membrane surrounded by a cell wall, they are much smaller than plant and animal cells, and their genetic material is a single DNA loop.
Plasmid
A small ring of DNA in the cytoplasm of a bacterial cell, separate from the single DNA loop. A bacterial cell may contain one or more plasmids.
Nucleus
The sub-cellular structure that encloses the genetic material of a plant or animal cell and controls the activities of the cell.
Cell membrane
The structure that surrounds the cytoplasm of a cell and controls the passage of substances into and out of the cell.
Cytoplasm
The jelly-like part of a cell in which most of the cell's chemical reactions take place and in which the sub-cellular structures are found.
Mitochondria

Sub-cellular structures in which aerobic respiration takes place, transferring the energy the cell needs to carry out its functions. Cells that need a great deal of energy, such as muscle cells, contain many mitochondria.
Ribosomes
Sub-cellular structures where protein synthesis takes place: amino acids are joined together to make the proteins the cell needs.
Chloroplast

A sub-cellular structure found in plant and algal cells that contains chlorophyll. The chlorophyll absorbs light so that the cell can carry out photosynthesis, so chloroplasts are found in plant cells that receive light rather than in every plant cell.
Permanent vacuole
A space in the cytoplasm of a plant cell that is filled with cell sap. It is one of the parts plant cells often have in addition to the parts found in animal cells.
Cell wall
A layer made of cellulose that surrounds the cell membrane of plant and algal cells and strengthens the cell. Animal cells do not have a cell wall.
Specialised cell
A cell whose structure enables it to carry out a particular function. Examples are sperm cells, nerve cells and muscle cells in animals, and root hair cells, xylem and phloem cells in plants.
Root hair cell
A specialised plant cell in the root with a long, thin extension into the soil. The extension increases the surface area of the cell for absorbing water and mineral ions.
Xylem and phloem cells

Specialised plant cells that form transport tissues. Xylem cells form hollow tubes with thickened walls that carry water and mineral ions from the roots; phloem cells form tubes with sieve plates that carry dissolved sugars through the plant.
Cell differentiation

The process in which a cell acquires different sub-cellular structures to enable it to carry out a certain function, so that it becomes a specialised cell. Most types of animal cell differentiate at an early stage, while many types of plant cell retain the ability to differentiate throughout life.
Magnification
How many times larger an image is than the real object, calculated using magnification = size of image / size of real object. The image size and the real size must be measured in the same units.
Resolving power

The ability of a microscope to show two points that are close together as separate points. An electron microscope has much higher magnification and resolving power than a light microscope, so it can be used to study cells in much finer detail.

chemistry-a-simple-model-of-the-atom-sym.d: Chemistry — A simple model of the atom, symbols, relative atomic mass, electronic charge and isotopes
terms: Atom
The smallest part of an element that can exist. All substances are made of atoms.
Element
A substance made of only one kind of atom. There are about 100 different elements, shown in the periodic table.
Chemical symbol
The one- or two-letter code used to represent an atom of an element, eg O represents an atom of oxygen and Na represents an atom of sodium.
Periodic table
The table in which the elements are shown; it is supplied in the exam.
Compound
A substance containing two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions, represented by a formula built from the symbols of the atoms it was formed from.
Chemical reaction
A change that always forms one or more new substances and often involves a detectable energy change. Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions.
Word equation
A representation of a reaction using the names of the reactants and products, with an arrow from reactants to products.
Balanced symbol equation
A representation of a reaction using symbols and formulae in which there are the same numbers of each type of atom on both sides.
Half equation
(HT only) An equation showing the electrons lost or gained by one species, eg 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻.
Ionic equation
(HT only) An equation showing only the ions and atoms that take part in the reaction, with spectator ions left out.
Mixture
Two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined together; the chemical properties of each substance in the mixture are unchanged.
Filtration
A physical process that separates an insoluble solid from a liquid; the solid stays on the filter paper as residue and the liquid passes through as filtrate.
Crystallisation
A physical process in which the solvent is evaporated from a solution so that the dissolved solid is left behind as crystals.
Simple distillation
A physical process that separates a solvent from a solution by boiling it off and condensing the vapour, leaving the dissolved solid behind.
Fractional distillation
A physical process that separates two or more miscible liquids using the differences between their boiling points.
Chromatography
A physical process that separates substances in a mixture by how they move with a solvent through paper.
Physical process
A separation method that involves no chemical reaction, so no new substances are made.
Scientific model
An idea used to explain observations; new experimental evidence may lead to a model being changed or replaced.
Plum pudding model
The model that followed the discovery of the electron: the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
Alpha particle scattering experiment
The experiment whose results led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom is concentrated at the centre (nucleus) and that the nucleus is charged.
Nuclear model
The model in which the mass of the atom is concentrated in a small charged nucleus; it replaced the plum pudding model.
Bohr model
Niels Bohr's adaptation of the nuclear model, in which electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances; his calculations agreed with experimental observations.
Proton
A positively charged particle in the nucleus; the positive charge of a nucleus is a whole number of these identical charges.
Neutron
An uncharged particle in the nucleus; the experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence for neutrons, about 20 years after the nucleus became accepted.
Electron
A negatively charged particle, relative charge −1, that occupies energy levels (shells) around the nucleus.
Relative electrical charge
Proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1.
Atomic number
The number of protons in an atom of an element. All atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons.
Atomic radius
Atoms are very small, having a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m).
Nucleus
The centre of the atom, containing almost all of its mass, with a radius less than 1/10 000 of that of the atom (about 1 x 10⁻¹⁴ m).
Relative mass of particles
Proton 1, neutron 1, electron very small.
Mass number
The sum of the protons and neutrons in an atom.
Isotopes
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
Ion
An atom that has lost or gained electrons, so the numbers of protons and electrons are no longer equal.
Relative atomic mass
An average value for an element that takes account of the abundance of its isotopes.
Energy level (shell)
A region around the nucleus that electrons occupy; electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels (innermost available shells) first.
Electronic structure
The arrangement of electrons in the energy levels of an atom, written as numbers such as 2,8,1 for sodium or drawn as a diagram.
System

A system is an object or a group of objects. It is simply whatever you choose to treat as the thing being studied — a single stone, a stone and the Earth together, or a kettle together with the water inside it. Choosing the system first is what makes it possible to say clearly which stores are emptying and which are filling.
Energy store

A way in which a system holds energy. Naming a store answers the question 'where is the energy now?' — for example the kinetic store, the gravitational potential store, the elastic potential store, the thermal store and the chemical store.
Kinetic store
The store filled when an object moves. The faster the object moves and the greater its mass, the more energy is in its kinetic store.
Gravitational potential store
The store filled when an object is raised. Its content depends on the mass of the object, its height, and the gravitational field strength.
Elastic potential store
The store filled when an object such as a spring, a rubber band or a crumpling car bumper is stretched, squashed or deformed.
Thermal store
The store filled when the temperature of a material rises. Almost every everyday change ends with energy in the thermal stores of the objects involved and of the surroundings.
Chemical store
The store held in fuels, foods and batteries, which empties when a chemical reaction such as burning or respiration takes place.
Energy transfer
The moving of energy from one store to another. A transfer is not itself a store: the routes named in this section are heating, work done by forces and work done when a current flows.
Heating
A transfer of energy caused by a difference in temperature. Heating fills the thermal store of the cooler object and empties the store supplying the energy.
Work done by a force
The transfer of energy that happens when a force moves an object through a distance along the line of the force. Work done is calculated using W = F s.
Work done when a current flows
The transfer of energy that happens when charge is pushed through a component by a power supply. The energy transferred in a time t is found from P = E / t.
Dissipation
The spreading out of energy into thermal stores of the surroundings, where it is no longer useful. The energy is still there; it is simply shared out too thinly to be used.
Common scale energy diagram
A diagram in which the energy in each store, before and after a change, is drawn as a bar using the same scale throughout, so that the redistribution of a fixed total can be seen at a glance.
Kinetic energy (Ek)
The energy stored in an object because it is moving. It is calculated from kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x (speed)^2, that is E_k = 1/2 m v^2, and it is zero when the object is at rest.
The kinetic energy equation

In E_k = 1/2 m v^2 the speed alone is squared, not the mass and not the product of the two. Doubling the speed of an object multiplies its kinetic energy by four, while doubling its mass only doubles the kinetic energy.
Units in the kinetic energy equation
Kinetic energy Ek is in joules, J; mass m is in kilograms, kg; speed v is in metres per second, m/s. A mass in grams or a speed in km/h must be converted first, or the answer will not be in joules.
The joule (J)

The unit of every energy store in this section: kinetic, elastic potential and gravitational potential energy are all measured in joules. The newton is a unit of force and the watt is a unit of power, so neither can be the unit of an energy calculation.
Elastic potential energy (Ee)

The energy stored in a spring, or other elastic object, because it has been stretched or compressed. For a spring it is calculated from elastic potential energy = 0.5 x spring constant x (extension)^2, that is E_e = 1/2 k e^2.
Spring constant (k)
A measure of how stiff a spring is: the force needed for each metre of extension. It is measured in newtons per metre, N/m, so a spring of large k needs a large force to stretch it a given amount.
Extension (e)

The increase in the length of the spring, measured in metres, m. It is the stretched length minus the original unstretched length, not the stretched length itself, and it must be converted from centimetres or millimetres before it is squared.
Limit of proportionality

The point beyond which extension is no longer proportional to the force applied. The equation E_e = 1/2 k e^2 is used only while the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded; past that point it no longer gives the energy stored.
Gravitational potential energy (Ep)

The energy stored in an object because of its position in a gravitational field. The amount gained when an object is raised is calculated from g.p.e. = mass x gravitational field strength x height, that is E_p = m g h.
Gravitational field strength (g)
The force acting on each kilogram of mass, measured in newtons per kilogram, N/kg. Its value is always supplied in the question in this specification, so it never has to be recalled.
Height (h)

The vertical distance the object is raised above ground level, measured in metres, m. When an object is moved along a slope or a ramp, it is the vertical rise that is used as h, not the longer distance travelled along the surface.
Units in the g.p.e. equation
In E_p = m g h the gravitational potential energy Ep is in joules, J; mass m is in kilograms, kg; gravitational field strength g is in newtons per kilogram, N/kg; and height h is in metres, m.
Units in the elastic potential energy equation
In E_e = 1/2 k e^2 the elastic potential energy Ee is in joules, J; the spring constant k is in newtons per metre, N/m; and the extension e is in metres, m.
Mass and weight

Mass is the quantity of matter in an object, measured in kilograms, kg, and it is m in E_k = 1/2 m v^2 and E_p = m g h. No mass appears in E_e = 1/2 k e^2. Weight is a force in newtons and is never substituted for the mass.
Choosing the right energy equation

Use E_k = 1/2 m v^2 when an object is moving, E_e = 1/2 k e^2 when a spring has been stretched, and E_p = m g h when an object has been raised. Only the kinetic and elastic equations contain a factor of 0.5.
System
The object, or group of objects, whose energy is being considered. In this section the system is the material whose temperature changes — for example a metal block, or the water in a beaker.
Change in thermal energy (∆E)
The energy stored in, or released from, a system as its temperature changes, measured in joules, J. It is a change, not a total: it does not say how much energy the system stores altogether.
Word equation for a temperature change
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change. All three factors multiply, so leaving one out, or dividing by one of them, makes the answer wrong by that whole factor.
∆E = m c ∆θ
The symbol form of the same equation: ∆E is the change in thermal energy, m the mass, c the specific heat capacity and ∆θ the temperature change. The symbol ∆ always means 'change in'.
Mass, m
The mass of the material whose temperature changes, in kilograms, kg. A mass given in grams must be divided by 1000 before it is used, because the unit of c already contains 'per kilogram'.
Specific heat capacity, c

The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius. It is a property of the substance, so every sample of that substance has the same value whatever its mass.
J/kg °C

The unit of specific heat capacity: joules per kilogram per degree Celsius. The unit is a direct reading of the definition — joules of energy, for each kilogram, for each degree Celsius of temperature rise.
Temperature change, ∆θ
The difference between the final and the starting temperature, in degrees Celsius, °C. It is found by subtraction before the equation is used, and it is never the final temperature on its own.
Required practical activity 1

An investigation to determine the specific heat capacity of one or more materials by linking the decrease of one energy store (or work done) to the rise in temperature and so to the increase in thermal energy stored. Measuring the energy supplied, the mass and the temperature rise gives c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ).
Energy transferred to the surroundings

Energy that leaves the heated block or liquid and warms the room instead. It makes the measured temperature rise smaller than the supplied energy alone would produce, so uninsulated apparatus gives a value of c that is too high.
Accurate measurement in this practical (AT 1 and AT 5)

The apparatus and technique skills this practical draws on: recording mass, temperature and time accurately (AT 1), and safely using apparatus such as an immersion heater and joulemeter to measure an energy transfer (AT 5).
Handling the equation and its units (WS and MS)

The mathematical and working-scientifically demands that arise here: converting grams to kilograms, making c the subject of ∆E = m c ∆θ, and evaluating how energy transferred to the surroundings affects the result.
power

Power is the rate at which energy is transferred, or the rate at which work is done. It is not a quantity of energy: it says how many joules are transferred each second, so a power value always needs both an energy and a time.
watt (W)
The watt is the unit of power, symbol W. An energy transfer of 1 joule per second is equal to a power of 1 watt, so 1 W is 1 J/s.
energy transferred (E)
The energy transferred, symbol E, is measured in joules, J. Divided by the time in seconds it gives the power: power = (energy transferred)/(time), [P = E/t].
work done (W)

Work done, symbol W, is measured in joules, J, because doing work is one way of transferring energy. Divided by the time it gives the power: power = (work done)/(time), [P = W/t]. The letter W is also the symbol for the watt; in P = W/t it stands for the work done.
time (t)
The time, symbol t, is measured in seconds, s. A time given in minutes or hours must be converted to seconds before it is used in P = E/t or P = W/t.
comparing powers

Two machines that transfer the same energy, for example two electric motors lifting the same weight through the same height, differ in power only through the time taken. The one that finishes sooner has the greater power.
Chromosome
A structure found in the nucleus of a cell, made of a DNA molecule. Each chromosome carries a large number of genes.
Gene
A section of a DNA molecule carried on a chromosome. A single chromosome carries a large number of genes, so genes are much smaller structures than chromosomes.
Pairs of chromosomes in body cells
In body cells the chromosomes are normally found in pairs, so each type of chromosome is present twice in the nucleus.
Cell cycle

The series of stages in which cells divide. During the cell cycle the genetic material is doubled and then divided into two identical cells. The three overall stages are growth with DNA replication, mitosis, and division of the cytoplasm and cell membranes.
Growth stage of the cell cycle

Before a cell can divide it needs to grow and increase the number of sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and mitochondria. In this stage the DNA replicates to form two copies of each chromosome.
Mitosis
The stage of the cell cycle in which one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides.
Division of the cytoplasm and cell membranes
The final stage of the cell cycle, in which the cytoplasm and cell membranes divide to form two identical cells.
Growth and development by mitosis
Cell division by mitosis is important in the growth and development of multicellular organisms, because it produces new cells that are identical to the parent cell.
Stem cell
An undifferentiated cell of an organism which is capable of giving rise to many more cells of the same type, and from which certain other cells can arise from differentiation.
Embryonic stem cells
Stem cells from human embryos, which can be cloned and made to differentiate into most different types of human cells.
Adult stem cells in bone marrow
Stem cells from adult bone marrow, which can form many types of cells including blood cells.
Meristem tissue
Tissue in plants that can differentiate into any type of plant cell, throughout the life of the plant.
Therapeutic cloning
A process in which an embryo is produced with the same genes as the patient. Stem cells from the embryo are not rejected by the patient's body so they may be used for medical treatment.
Cloning plants from meristems

Stem cells from meristems in plants can be used to produce clones of plants quickly and economically. Rare species can be cloned to protect them from extinction, and crop plants with special features such as disease resistance can be cloned to produce large numbers of identical plants for farmers.
Periodic table
The arrangement of all the elements in order of atomic (proton) number, set out so that elements with similar properties fall in the same column.
Group
A column of the periodic table. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons and so have similar chemical properties.
Period
A row of the periodic table. The period number equals the number of occupied electron shells in an atom of the element.
Atomic (proton) number
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. It fixes the element's place in the periodic table.
Outer electrons
The electrons in the highest occupied shell of an atom. Their number decides the group and controls the element's chemical reactions.
Periodicity
The repeating of similar properties at regular intervals along the order of elements, which is why the table is called periodic.
Atomic weight
The mass measure used to order elements before subatomic particles were known; now called relative atomic mass.
Mendeleev's gaps
Spaces left in his table for elements he believed had not yet been discovered, with properties predicted from the neighbouring elements.
Isotopes
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, which is why atomic weight does not always rise with proton number.
Metal
An element that reacts to form positive ions. Metals lie to the left and towards the bottom of the periodic table.
Non-metal
An element that does not form positive ions. Non-metals lie towards the right and top of the periodic table.
Positive ion
An ion formed when an atom loses one or more electrons, leaving more protons than electrons.
Noble gases
The elements of Group 0. They are unreactive and do not easily form molecules because their atoms have stable electron arrangements.
Stable electron arrangement
An outer shell holding eight electrons, or two in the case of helium, so the atom has no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons.
Boiling point trend in Group 0
Boiling points increase with increasing relative atomic mass, that is, going down the group.
Alkali metals
The elements of Group 1. Their characteristic properties follow from the single electron in the outer shell of their atoms.
Metal hydroxide
The alkaline compound produced, along with hydrogen, when a Group 1 metal reacts with water.
Reactivity trend in Group 1
Reactivity increases going down the group, as the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost.
Halogens
The elements of Group 7. They are non-metals with seven outer electrons whose atoms go about in pairs as molecules.
Diatomic molecule
A molecule made of two atoms joined together, the form in which the halogen elements exist, such as Cl2 and Br2.
Metal halide
The ionic compound formed when a halogen reacts with a metal, such as sodium chloride or iron bromide.
Molecular halide
The covalent compound formed when a halogen reacts with a non-metal, such as hydrogen chloride.
Reactivity trend in Group 7
Reactivity decreases going down the group, as the outer shell is further from the nucleus and an electron is gained less easily.
Displacement reaction
A reaction in which a more reactive halogen takes the place of a less reactive halogen in an aqueous solution of its salt.

physics-conservation-and-dissipation-of-.d: Physics — Conservation and dissipation of energy
terms: Conservation of energy
Energy can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated, but it cannot be created or destroyed. The total energy before a change is always equal to the total energy after it.
Closed system
A system in which no energy enters or leaves. Energy can still be transferred between the stores inside a closed system, but there is no net change to the total energy of the system.
Dissipation
The spreading out of energy into stores that are less useful, most often the thermal store of the surroundings. Energy is dissipated in all system changes.
Wasted energy

The everyday name for energy that has been dissipated. It has not been destroyed; it has been stored in a way that cannot be used for the intended purpose, for example in the thermal store of a warm motor.
Lubrication
Putting a substance such as oil between surfaces that move over each other. The friction between the surfaces is reduced, so less energy is dissipated to thermal stores as the machine runs.
Thermal insulation
A layer of material of low thermal conductivity placed around an object or a building to reduce the rate of energy transfer by conduction to the surroundings.
Thermal conductivity
A property of a material, used here only as a comparison: the higher the thermal conductivity of a material, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across the material.
Rate of cooling of a building
How quickly a building transfers energy to colder surroundings. The rate of cooling is lower when the walls are thicker and when the walls are made of a material with a lower thermal conductivity.
Required practical activity 2

An investigation of the effectiveness of different materials as thermal insulators, and of the factors that affect the thermal insulation properties of a material, such as the thickness of the layer and the number of layers used.
Control variables in the insulation practical

The quantities kept the same so that only the material or the thickness affects the result: the volume and starting temperature of the water, the size of the container, the room temperature and the time over which the temperature is measured.
AT 1 and AT 5 in this practical

AT 1 is the use of appropriate apparatus to make and record measurements of length, temperature and time; AT 5 is making measurements of energy and temperature changes. Both are exercised by measuring the thickness of the insulating layer with a ruler and by recording the fall in water temperature at set times.
Repeats, means and anomalies

Working scientifically and mathematical skills developed in this practical: taking repeat readings for each material, identifying anomalous results, calculating a mean temperature drop and plotting the results so that materials can be compared.
Energy efficiency

The share of the energy supplied to a device that is transferred usefully. The energy efficiency for any energy transfer can be calculated using the equation: efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer). Efficiency is a ratio, so it has no unit and can never be greater than 1.
Efficiency from power
Efficiency may also be calculated using the equation: efficiency = (useful power output)/(total power input). Both powers must be in the same unit, and the answer is again a ratio with no unit.
Increasing efficiency

Making a larger share of the input energy transfer useful by reducing the unwanted transfers: lubricating moving parts, insulating hot components, streamlining a moving object to reduce air resistance and using thicker wires of lower resistance.
Diffusion

The spreading out of the particles of any substance in solution, or particles of a gas, resulting in a net movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration. Substances may move into and out of cells across the cell membranes via diffusion, and no energy from respiration is needed.
Concentration gradient

The difference in concentrations of a substance between two areas. Diffusion gives a net movement down a concentration gradient, from the area of higher concentration to the area of lower concentration; the greater the difference in concentrations, the faster the rate of diffusion.
Factors affecting the rate of diffusion

The factors which affect the rate of diffusion are the difference in concentrations (concentration gradient), the temperature, and the surface area of the membrane. Increasing any one of these increases the rate of diffusion.
Substances transported by diffusion

Substances transported in and out of cells by diffusion include oxygen and carbon dioxide in gas exchange, and the waste product urea, which moves from cells into the blood plasma for excretion in the kidney.
Surface area to volume ratio

The surface area of an organism or cell compared with its volume. A single-celled organism has a relatively large surface area to volume ratio, which allows sufficient transport of molecules into and out of the cell to meet the needs of the organism. The ratio gets smaller as an organism gets larger.
Exchange surface

A surface in a multicellular organism that is specialised for exchanging materials, so that sufficient molecules can be transported into and out of cells for the organism's needs. Its effectiveness is increased by having a large surface area, a membrane that is thin, (in animals) an efficient blood supply and, in animals for gaseous exchange, being ventilated.
Short diffusion path
The short distance a substance has to travel across an exchange surface. A membrane that is thin provides a short diffusion path, which increases the effectiveness of the exchange surface.
Adaptations for exchanging materials

The small intestine and lungs in mammals, gills in fish, and the roots and leaves in plants are adapted for exchange by having a large surface area and a thin membrane that gives a short diffusion path. The small intestine, lungs and gills also have an efficient blood supply, and the lungs are ventilated.
Osmosis
The diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane. Water may move across cell membranes via osmosis.
Partially permeable membrane
A membrane that allows water molecules through but not all of the dissolved solute particles. Osmosis is the diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane.
Active transport
The movement of substances from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution, that is against a concentration gradient. This requires energy from respiration.
Mineral ion uptake by root hairs
Active transport allows mineral ions to be absorbed into plant root hairs from very dilute solutions in the soil, against a concentration gradient. Plants require ions for healthy growth.
Sugar absorption from the gut
Active transport allows sugar molecules to be absorbed from lower concentrations in the gut into the blood, which has a higher sugar concentration. Sugar molecules are used for cell respiration.

physics-national-and-global-energy-resou.d: Physics — National and global energy resources
terms: Energy resource

A supply of energy that people can draw on. The main energy resources available for use on Earth include fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas), nuclear fuel, bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves. Electricity is not an energy resource: it has to be generated using one of these resources.
Fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas)

The three fossil fuels named by the specification. They formed from the remains of living things over many millions of years and are burned to release energy. They are non-renewable: they are not replenished on any timescale that matters against the rate at which they are used.
Nuclear fuel
Uranium (or plutonium) used as a fuel in nuclear power stations. It is mined from rock but it is not a fossil fuel, and it is non-renewable because the fuel is not replenished as it is used.
Bio-fuel
Fuel made from plant or animal material, for example wood, crops grown for fuel, or waste. It is renewable because the crops used can be grown again as the fuel is used.
Wind

Moving air, used as an energy resource mainly for electricity generation. It is renewable, and it is unreliable in the sense that its output rises and falls with the weather and cannot be turned up on demand.
Hydro-electricity

An energy resource that uses water stored behind a dam, usually in a river valley. It is renewable, because rain refills the reservoir, and it is comparatively reliable because the stored water can be released when it is wanted.
Geothermal
An energy resource that uses the energy of hot rock beneath the Earth's surface. It is renewable and available at all hours, but it is only practical where hot rock lies close enough to the surface.
The tides

The twice-daily rise and fall of the sea, caused by the Moon and the Sun rather than by the weather. Tidal energy is renewable and reliable, because the times of high and low water are known in advance.
The Sun

The Sun is an energy resource in its own right. Its energy can be used for heating (for example warming water directly) as well as for electricity generation. It is renewable, and its output varies with the time of day, the season and the cloud.
Water waves
Waves on the surface of the sea, raised by the wind. Wave energy is renewable and is a separate resource from both hydro-electricity and the tides.
Renewable energy resource

A renewable energy resource is one that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used. The test is replacement keeping pace with use - not the size of the supply, not the price, and not whether the resource is clean.
Non-renewable energy resource
A resource that is not replenished as it is used, so the supply falls as it is drawn on. Coal, oil, gas and nuclear fuel are non-renewable.
Use: transport
Moving people and goods. Worldwide, transport runs overwhelmingly on oil, as petrol and diesel; bio-fuel and electricity supply smaller shares.
Use: electricity generation
Producing electricity for the mains supply. Almost every resource on the specification's list can be used this way, which is why electricity itself is not a resource.
Use: heating
Warming homes, water and industrial processes. Gas, oil, bio-fuel, geothermal and the Sun are all used for heating directly, without any electricity being generated first.
Reliability of an energy resource

How dependably a resource can supply energy when it is wanted. Fossil fuels, nuclear fuel and geothermal can be run whenever they are needed; the tides are predictable in advance; wind, the Sun and water waves depend on the weather. Reliability is about availability on demand, not about how much energy the resource gives out.
Environmental impact

The damage done by obtaining and using a resource: carbon dioxide from burning fuels, sulfur dioxide leading to acid rain, radioactive waste from nuclear fuel, and land, habitat and landscape effects from dams, wind farms and fuel crops. Every resource has some impact.
Trends in the use of energy resources

Patterns over time, such as the rising share of wind and solar, the decline of coal, and the continued dominance of oil in transport. Trends are driven by cost, by concern about environmental impact and by government decisions.
Political, social, ethical and economic considerations

The non-scientific factors that decide whether an environmental issue is acted on. Science can identify an issue but does not always have the power to deal with it, because cost, jobs, public opinion, fairness between countries and government policy all bear on what is actually done.
cell
The basic building block from which all living organisms are made.
tissue
A group of cells with a similar structure and function.
organ
An aggregation of tissues performing specific functions.
organ system
A group of organs that organs are organised into; organ systems work together to form organisms.

chemistry-chemical-bonds-ionic-covalent-.d: Chemistry — Chemical bonds, ionic, covalent and metallic
terms: Strong chemical bond

There are three types of strong chemical bond: ionic, covalent and metallic. All three are electrostatic in origin, but they differ in which particles are held together and in what happens to the outer electrons.
Ionic bonding
Bonding in which the particles are oppositely charged ions. It occurs in compounds formed from metals combined with non-metals.
Covalent bonding
Bonding in which the particles are atoms which share pairs of electrons. It occurs in most non-metallic elements and in compounds of non-metals.
Metallic bonding
Bonding in which the particles are atoms which share delocalised electrons. It occurs in metallic elements and in alloys.
Electrostatic force

The force of attraction between opposite electric charges. Chemical bonding is explained by electrostatic attraction: between positive and negative ions, between two nuclei and a shared pair of electrons, or between metal ions and the sea of delocalised electrons.
Electron transfer
The movement of electrons from the outer shell of a metal atom to the outer shell of a non-metal atom when the two react. Transfer produces ions; it is not itself the bond.
Positive ion
An ion formed when a metal atom loses one or more electrons from its outer shell. It has more protons than electrons, so its charge is positive.
Negative ion
An ion formed when a non-metal atom gains one or more electrons into its outer shell. It has more electrons than protons, so its charge is negative.
Noble gas electronic structure
The full outer shell arrangement of a Group 0 element. The ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and by non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 have the electronic structure of a noble gas.
Dot and cross diagram
A diagram that shows the electron transfer forming an ionic compound, using dots for the electrons of one atom and crosses for the other, so that the origin of each electron can be followed.
Group number and ionic charge
For the elements in scope, the charge on the ion follows from the group number: Group 1 forms 1+, Group 2 forms 2+, Group 6 forms 2- and Group 7 forms 1-.
Giant ionic structure
An ionic compound is a giant structure of ions, held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions. There are no separate molecules in it.
Forces acting in all directions
In an ionic lattice the electrostatic forces act in all directions, not along a fixed line between two chosen ions. This is what is meant by ionic bonding.
Representations of sodium chloride
The structure of sodium chloride can be shown as a two-dimensional diagram, as a three-dimensional ball and stick model or as a space-filling model. Each is a model of the same giant lattice.
Empirical formula of an ionic compound
The simplest whole number ratio of the ions in the structure. It is worked out from a model or diagram by counting the ions of each type and cancelling to the simplest ratio.
Limitations of ionic models

A ball and stick model shows gaps between ions that do not exist and sticks that are not real; a two-dimensional diagram shows forces in only two directions; no diagram can show the full extent of the lattice.
Strength of a covalent bond

When atoms share pairs of electrons they form covalent bonds, and these bonds between atoms are strong. The strength of the bonds inside a molecule says nothing about the melting or boiling point of the substance.
Small molecule
A covalently bonded substance may consist of small molecules, each containing a small fixed number of non-metal atoms, such as H2, Cl2, HCl, H2O, NH3, CH4 and CO2.
Polymer
A covalently bonded substance whose molecules are very large: many small molecules joined into long chains. A polymer has very large molecules, not a giant structure.
Giant covalent structure
A structure in which very many atoms are joined by covalent bonds throughout the whole structure, with no separate molecules. Diamond and silicon dioxide are the specification's examples.
Dot and cross diagram of a molecule

A diagram showing the shared pairs of electrons in a molecule, using dots and crosses to show which atom each electron came from. Required for hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen chloride, water, ammonia and methane.
Repeating unit and n
A polymer is represented by its repeating unit drawn in brackets with a subscript n, where n is a large number. It is not a value to be calculated from the diagram.
Line representing a single bond
In a displayed formula or a diagram of a giant structure, one line between two atoms represents one single covalent bond, that is one shared pair of electrons.
Limitations of molecular models
A dot and cross diagram shows the electrons but not the shape or size; a two-dimensional diagram flattens a three-dimensional molecule; a ball and stick model exaggerates the space between atoms.
Molecular formula from a model
The molecular formula is deduced by counting the atoms of each element shown in the model or diagram. The bonds, sticks or lines are not counted, and the number is not reduced to the simplest ratio.
Giant metallic structure
Metals consist of giant structures of atoms arranged in a regular pattern.
Delocalised electron

An electron from the outer shell of a metal atom that is no longer held by one atom and is free to move through the whole structure. Sharing these delocalised electrons gives rise to strong metallic bonds.
Alloy
A mixture containing a metal and one or more other elements. The bonding in an alloy is metallic, as it is in a pure metallic element.

physics-current-potential-difference-and.d: Physics — Current, potential difference and resistance
terms: Standard circuit symbols

Circuit diagrams use standard symbols, so that any circuit can be read by anyone. The symbols needed are: open switch, closed switch, cell, battery, diode, resistor, variable resistor, LED, lamp, fuse, voltmeter, ammeter, thermistor and LDR. A cell is one long thin line beside one short thick line; a battery is two or more cells drawn in line. A resistor is a plain rectangle; a variable resistor is that rectangle with an arrow drawn diagonally across it. An ammeter is a circle containing A; a voltmeter is a circle containing V.
Drawing and interpreting circuit diagrams

To draw a circuit diagram, components are joined by straight lines standing for connecting wires, with each component shown by its correct standard symbol. To interpret one, trace the loops: components on the same single loop are in series and carry the same current, while components on separate branches are in parallel. An ammeter is always drawn in the loop with the component whose current is being measured; a voltmeter is always drawn as a separate branch across the component.
Source of potential difference

For electrical charge to flow through a closed circuit the circuit must include a source of potential difference, such as a cell, a battery or a power supply. A complete loop on its own is not enough: with nothing to push the charges round, the current is zero. The source does not create the charges — they are already in the metal — it provides the potential difference that makes them drift one way.
Electric current

Electric current is a flow of electrical charge. The size of the electric current is the rate of flow of electrical charge, that is, how much charge passes a point each second. It is not a flow of energy, and it is not the speed of the individual electrons, which drift very slowly even when the current is large.
Charge flow equation Q = I t

Charge flow, current and time are linked by the equation charge flow = current × time, written [Q = I t]. Rearranged, I = Q ÷ t and t = Q ÷ I. The time must be in seconds before it is substituted, so minutes and hours have to be converted first: 5.0 minutes is 300 s.
Coulomb (C)
Charge flow, Q, is measured in coulombs, C. The coulomb is a quantity of charge, not a rate: one coulomb passes a point when a current of one ampere flows for one second.
Ampere (A)

Current, I, is measured in amperes, A; amp is acceptable for ampere. One ampere is a flow of one coulomb of charge each second, so the ampere measures a rate of flow of charge while the coulomb measures an amount of charge.
Time in seconds

Time, t, is measured in seconds, s. Because the equations of this section are defined with time in seconds, any time given in minutes or hours must be converted before substitution: multiply minutes by 60 and hours by 3600.
Current in a single closed loop

A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop. Charge is not used up as it goes round, so an ammeter placed anywhere in that loop gives the same reading, whether it is before, between or after the components. What the components use is energy, not charge.
Resistance

The current through a component depends on both the resistance of the component and the potential difference across it. Resistance opposes the flow of charge: the greater the resistance of the component, the smaller the current for a given pd across it. The current can therefore be changed either by changing the pd or by changing the resistance.
Potential difference (pd)

Potential difference, V, is measured in volts, V. It is the quantity that drives charge round a circuit, and it is measured across a component rather than through it. Questions are set using the term potential difference; a student who writes voltage instead gains credit, because voltage is an accepted alternative name for the same quantity.
The equation V = I R

Current, potential difference or resistance can be calculated using the equation potential difference = current × resistance, written [V = I R]. Rearranged, I = V ÷ R and R = V ÷ I. To find a resistance you divide the pd by the current; multiplying them instead is the commonest error in this topic.
Ohm (Ω)

Resistance, R, is measured in ohms, Ω. One ohm is the resistance of a component that has a pd of one volt across it when a current of one ampere passes through it, which follows directly from R = V ÷ I.
Required practical activity 3

Circuit diagrams are used to set up and check appropriate circuits to investigate the factors affecting the resistance of electrical circuits. The standard arrangement puts an ammeter in the loop with the test component and a voltmeter across it; the resistance is then calculated from R = V ÷ I. The two factors investigated are the length of a wire at constant temperature, and combinations of resistors in series and parallel.
Resistance and the length of a wire

For a wire at constant temperature, resistance is directly proportional to length: doubling the length doubles the resistance, and a graph of resistance against length is a straight line through the origin. The temperature must be held constant, which is why the current is kept small and the circuit is switched off between readings — a wire that warms up has a higher resistance, which would spoil the pattern.
Resistors in series and in parallel

Resistors joined in series have a combined resistance larger than either one alone, because the charge must pass through both. Resistors joined in parallel have a combined resistance smaller than either one alone, because the charge now has more than one path to take; two identical resistors in parallel give half the resistance of one.
Ohmic conductor

The current through an ohmic conductor at a constant temperature is directly proportional to the potential difference across the resistor, which means that the resistance remains constant as the current changes. Its I–V graph is a straight line through the origin. A fixed resistor kept at constant temperature is the standard example.
Components with non-constant resistance

For some resistors the value of R remains constant, but in others it can change as the current changes. The resistance of components such as lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs is not constant; it changes with the current through the component. Their I–V graphs are therefore not straight lines through the origin.
Filament lamp

The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases. A larger current heats the filament more, so its resistance rises and its I–V graph bends over into an S-shape, becoming less steep as the pd increases. A filament lamp is therefore not an ohmic conductor.
Diode

The current through a diode flows in one direction only. The diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction, so the reverse current is very nearly zero. In the forward direction it conducts, but only once the pd is large enough, so its I–V graph lies flat along the reverse side and then rises steeply forward.
Thermistor

The resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases. This is the opposite of the behaviour of a metal wire, whose resistance rises when it is heated, and it is what makes the thermistor useful as a temperature sensor.
Thermistors in circuits

In a thermostat the thermistor senses the room temperature. When the room cools, the thermistor's resistance rises; the circuit detects that change and switches the heater on. When the room warms again the resistance falls and the heater is switched off, so the temperature is held near a set value. The same idea is used in fire alarms and in engine temperature sensors.
Light-dependent resistor (LDR)

The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases. In bright light its resistance may be only a few hundred ohms; in darkness it can be millions of ohms. It is therefore used as a light sensor.
LDRs in circuits

An LDR is used to switch lights on when it gets dark. As darkness falls, the light intensity on the LDR drops, so its resistance rises; the circuit senses that change and switches the street lamp on. At dawn the resistance falls again and the lamp is switched off. The same arrangement is used in automatic camera exposure and in burglar alarms.
Circuit to measure resistance

To measure the resistance of a component, an ammeter is placed in the loop with the component so that it measures the current through it, and a voltmeter is placed across the component so that it measures the potential difference across it. The resistance is then calculated from R = V ÷ I. The circuit diagram is drawn using correct circuit symbols; a variable resistor or a variable power supply lets several pairs of readings be taken.
Linear and non-linear circuit elements

Graphs are used to explore whether circuit elements are linear or non-linear. A linear element gives a straight-line I–V graph through the origin and has constant resistance; a non-linear element gives a curve, and its resistance changes. The shape relates to the function of the component: the lamp's curve flattens because the filament heats up, and the diode's graph is flat on one side because it conducts one way only.
Required practical activity 4

Circuit diagrams are used to construct appropriate circuits to investigate the I–V characteristics of a variety of circuit elements, including a filament lamp, a diode and a resistor at constant temperature. Readings of current and pd are taken over a range of values, including reversed ones, and plotted as I against V. The resistor must be kept at constant temperature so that heating does not change the resistance being measured.

biology-animal-tissues-organs-and-organ-.d: Biology — Animal tissues, organs and organ systems
terms: Digestive system
An organ system in which several organs work together to digest and absorb food.
Enzyme
A large protein molecule that acts as a biological catalyst, speeding up a reaction in a living organism without being changed by it.
Active site
The part of an enzyme molecule that the substrate fits into. Its shape means the enzyme catalyses only one specific reaction.
Lock and key theory
A simplified model of enzyme action in which the substrate (the key) fits into the active site of the enzyme (the lock).
Denaturing
The change in the shape of an enzyme's active site caused by a high temperature or the wrong pH, so that the substrate no longer fits and the reaction stops.
Metabolism
The sum of all the reactions in a cell or in the body. These reactions are catalysed by enzymes.
Digestion
The breakdown of food by digestive enzymes into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the bloodstream.
Carbohydrase and amylase
A carbohydrase is an enzyme that breaks down carbohydrates to simple sugars. Amylase is a carbohydrase which breaks down starch.
Protease
An enzyme that breaks down proteins to amino acids.
Lipase
An enzyme that breaks down lipids (fats) to glycerol and fatty acids.
Sites of production of digestive enzymes

Amylase is produced in the salivary glands, the pancreas and the small intestine. Protease is produced in the stomach, the pancreas and the small intestine. Lipase is produced in the pancreas and the small intestine.
Products of digestion
The small soluble molecules produced by digestion. They are used to build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins, and some glucose is used in respiration.
Bile

An alkaline liquid made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It neutralises hydrochloric acid from the stomach and emulsifies fat to form small droplets, which increases the surface area. The alkaline conditions and large surface area increase the rate of fat breakdown by lipase.
Heart
An organ that pumps blood around the body. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs, where gas exchange takes place, and the left ventricle pumps blood around the rest of the body.
Double circulatory system
A circulation in which the blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit of the body: once on the way to the lungs and once on the way to the rest of the body.
Blood vessels associated with the heart

The vena cava carries blood into the heart from the body and the pulmonary artery carries blood from the heart to the lungs. The pulmonary vein carries blood from the lungs back to the heart and the aorta carries blood from the heart to the body. The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself.
Structures of the lungs
Air passes down the trachea, into the bronchi and then into the alveoli, which are surrounded by a capillary network.
Alveoli
The tiny air sacs of the lungs, adapted for gaseous exchange by a large surface area, thin walls and the capillary network that surrounds them.
Pacemaker
A group of cells located in the right atrium that controls the natural resting heart rate. Artificial pacemakers are electrical devices used to correct irregularities in the heart rate.
Artery
A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart. Its wall is thick, containing muscle and elastic fibres, so that it withstands the high pressure of the blood.
Vein
A blood vessel that carries blood back towards the heart. Its wall is thin and it contains valves, because the blood is at low pressure.
Capillary
A very narrow blood vessel with a wall one cell thick, so that substances can pass quickly between the blood and the tissues.
Blood
A tissue consisting of plasma, in which the red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets are suspended.
Plasma
The liquid part of the blood, which transports the blood cells and dissolved substances around the body.
Red blood cell
A blood cell that carries oxygen. It contains haemoglobin, has no nucleus and is a biconcave disc, giving a large surface area for the uptake of oxygen.
White blood cell
A blood cell that defends the body against pathogens, for example by engulfing them or by producing antibodies.
Platelet
A small fragment of cell suspended in the plasma that helps the blood to clot at a wound.
Coronary heart disease

A disease in which layers of fatty material build up inside the coronary arteries, narrowing them. This reduces the flow of blood through the coronary arteries, resulting in a lack of oxygen for the heart muscle.
Stents and statins
Stents are used to keep the coronary arteries open. Statins are widely used to reduce blood cholesterol levels, which slows down the rate of fatty material deposit.
Faulty heart valve
A heart valve that does not open fully, or that develops a leak, so that less blood is pumped or blood flows the wrong way. Faulty heart valves can be replaced using biological or mechanical valves.
Heart transplant and artificial heart

In the case of heart failure a donor heart, or heart and lungs, can be transplanted. Artificial hearts are occasionally used to keep patients alive whilst waiting for a heart transplant, or to allow the heart to rest as an aid to recovery.
Health
The state of physical and mental well-being.
Communicable and non-communicable disease
Communicable diseases can be passed from one person to another, while non-communicable diseases cannot. Both are major causes of ill health.
Interaction of diseases

Different types of disease may interact, for example defects in the immune system make infectious disease more likely, viruses living in cells can trigger cancers, and severe physical ill health can lead to depression and other mental illness.
Risk factor
Something that is linked to an increased rate of a disease. Risk factors can be aspects of a person's lifestyle, or substances in the person's body or environment.
Causal mechanism

An explanation of how a risk factor brings about a disease. A causal mechanism has been proven for some risk factors, but not in others, and many diseases are caused by the interaction of a number of factors.
Sampling
Choosing a sample that is large enough and representative of the whole population, so that conclusions drawn from scientific data, including epidemiological data, are reliable.
Cancer
The result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division.
Benign and malignant tumours

Benign tumours are growths of abnormal cells which are contained in one area, usually within a membrane, and do not invade other parts of the body. Malignant tumour cells are cancers: they invade neighbouring tissues and spread to different parts of the body in the blood, where they form secondary tumours.
Risk factors for cancer
Lifestyle risk factors have been identified for various types of cancer, and there are also genetic risk factors for some cancers.
Key Stage 3 digestion (assumed knowledge)

Knowledge of the digestive system from Key Stage 3 science is assumed: food passes through the mouth, stomach and small intestine, where it is broken down, and the small soluble products are absorbed in the small intestine.
Word equation

A reaction written using the names of the substances rather than formulae, for example starch to sugars, or lipids to glycerol and fatty acids. Simple word equations should be understood; no chemical symbol equations are required.

chemistry-how-bonding-and-structure-are-.d: Chemistry — How bonding and structure are related to the properties of substances
terms: Solid
The state in which particles are packed closely in a fixed arrangement, so a solid keeps its own shape and volume.
Liquid
The state in which particles are still close together but can move past one another, so a liquid has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container.
Gas
The state in which particles are far apart and move randomly, so a gas fills whatever container it is put in.
Melting point
The one temperature at which a substance melts and at which it also freezes. Solid to liquid and liquid to solid both happen at this temperature.
Boiling point
The one temperature at which a substance boils and at which it also condenses. Liquid to gas and gas to liquid both happen at this temperature.
Simple model of the three states
A model in which the particles of a substance are represented by small solid spheres, arranged closely and regularly in a solid, closely but randomly in a liquid, and far apart in a gas.
Forces between particles
The attractions holding the particles of a substance to one another. Their strength depends on the type of bonding and the structure of the substance.
Energy needed to change state
The energy that must be supplied to separate particles from one another. The stronger the forces between the particles, the more energy is needed and the higher the melting point and boiling point.
Limitations of the simple model
(HT only) In the simple model there are no forces between the particles, all particles are shown as spheres, and the spheres are shown as solid.
Bulk property
A property such as melting point, colour, hardness or electrical conductivity that belongs to a large collection of particles arranged in a structure, not to a single atom.
State symbol
The letter or letters written in brackets after a formula in a chemical equation to show the state of that substance: (s) for solid, (l) for liquid and (g) for gas.
Aqueous solution (aq)
A solution made by dissolving a substance in water. It is shown in an equation by the state symbol (aq).
Giant ionic lattice
The regular structure formed by an ionic compound, in which very many oppositely charged ions are held in a repeating three-dimensional arrangement.
Electrostatic force of attraction
The attraction between oppositely charged ions. In a giant ionic lattice these forces are strong and act in all directions.
High melting and boiling points of ionic compounds
Ionic compounds melt and boil at high temperatures because large amounts of energy are needed to break the many strong bonds in the lattice.
Conduction by mobile ions
When an ionic compound is melted or dissolved in water the ions become free to move, so charge can flow and the substance conducts electricity.
Substance made of small molecules
A substance whose particles are small groups of atoms joined by covalent bonds. Such substances are usually gases or liquids with relatively low melting and boiling points.
Intermolecular force
The weak force of attraction between one molecule and another. It is these forces, not the covalent bonds, that are overcome when a molecular substance melts or boils.
Covalent bond
A strong bond formed by a shared pair of electrons between two atoms inside a molecule.
No overall electric charge
Molecules are neutral, so a molecular substance has no charged particles that are free to move and it does not conduct electricity.
Molecule size and intermolecular forces
Intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules, so larger molecules have higher melting and boiling points.
Polymer
A substance whose molecules are very large. The atoms in a polymer molecule are joined to other atoms by strong covalent bonds, usually forming a long chain.
Why polymers are solids at room temperature
Because polymer molecules are very large, the intermolecular forces between them are relatively strong, so polymers are solids at room temperature.
Giant covalent structure
A structure in which all of the atoms are linked to other atoms by strong covalent bonds throughout the whole structure. These bonds must be overcome to melt or boil the substance.
Examples of giant covalent structures
Diamond and graphite, which are forms of carbon, and silicon dioxide, also called silica.
Metallic bonding
The strong bonding in the giant structure of atoms that makes up a metal. It means that most metals have high melting and boiling points.
Layers of atoms in a pure metal
In a pure metal the atoms are arranged in layers. The layers can slide over one another, which allows metals to be bent and shaped.
Alloy
A mixture of a metal with other metals. Pure metals are too soft for many uses, so they are mixed to make alloys, which are harder.
Delocalised electrons
Electrons in a metal that are free to move through the whole structure. They carry electrical charge through the metal, so metals conduct electricity well.
Thermal conduction in metals
Metals are good conductors of thermal energy because energy is transferred through the metal by the delocalised electrons.
Predicting a state from data
A substance is solid below its melting point, liquid between its melting point and its boiling point, and gas above its boiling point.
Series connection

Components are in series when they are joined one after another in a single loop, so there is only one path for charge. Every charge that passes through one component must pass through all the others.
Parallel connection
Components are in parallel when they are joined side by side between the same two points, so the charge has a choice of paths. Each component sits on its own branch of the circuit.
Junction
A point in a circuit where the conducting path divides or rejoins. Charge that arrives at a junction each second equals the charge that leaves it each second, so no charge is created or lost there.
Current in a series circuit
In series there is the same current through each component, because there is only one path and charge is not used up. Moving an ammeter to a different place in the loop does not change its reading.
Sharing of potential difference in series
The total potential difference of the power supply is shared between components connected in series, so the separate potential differences add up to the supply potential difference.
Total resistance in series
The total resistance of two components in series is the sum of the resistance of each component, R_total = R_1 + R_2, because the charge has to pass through both in turn.
Potential difference in parallel
The potential difference across each component connected in parallel is the same, because the ends of every branch are joined to the same two points in the circuit.
Total current in a parallel circuit
The total current through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components, because the current from the supply divides between the branches and rejoins afterwards.
Total resistance in parallel
The total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor, because the second resistor gives the charge an extra path to flow along.
Ohm
The unit of resistance, R, is the ohm, symbol Ω. A component has a resistance of one ohm when a potential difference of one volt across it drives a current of one ampere through it.
Equivalent resistance
A single resistance that could replace a group of resistors without changing the current drawn from the supply. For resistors in series it is found by adding the individual resistances.
Ammeter in a circuit
An ammeter measures current and is connected in series with the component whose current is wanted, so that the same current passes through both the meter and that component.
Voltmeter in a circuit
A voltmeter measures potential difference and is connected in parallel with the component, that is across its two ends, so it experiences the same potential difference as that component.
dc supply
A direct current supply, such as a cell or battery, drives charge around the circuit in one direction only. The dc series circuits used for measurement and testing are built from such a supply.
Mixed circuit
A circuit that contains both series and parallel parts, for example a resistor in series with a pair of lamps that are in parallel with each other.
Variable resistor in a test circuit
A resistor whose resistance can be changed. Placed in series in a test circuit it alters the current, so several pairs of current and potential difference readings can be taken for one component.

biology-plant-tissues-organs-and-systems.d: Biology — Plant tissues, organs and systems
terms: Epidermal tissue
The tissue that covers the outer surfaces of a plant. In a leaf it forms the upper and lower epidermis, a protective covering that contains the guard cells surrounding the stomata.
Palisade mesophyll
The leaf tissue lying just below the upper epidermis. Its closely packed cells contain many chloroplasts, so this is the main tissue in which photosynthesis takes place.
Spongy mesophyll
The leaf tissue lying below the palisade mesophyll. Its cells are loosely packed with air spaces between them, so gases can diffuse to and from the photosynthesising cells.
Meristem tissue
Plant tissue found at the growing tips of shoots and roots. Its cells divide to produce the new cells a plant needs for growth.
Xylem tissue

The tissue that transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the stems and leaves. It is composed of hollow tubes strengthened by lignin, adapted for the transport of water in the transpiration stream.
Phloem tissue

The tissue that transports dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant for immediate use or storage. It is composed of tubes of elongated cells, and cell sap can move from one phloem cell to the next through pores in the end walls.
Translocation
The movement of food molecules, as dissolved sugars, through phloem tissue from the leaves to the rest of the plant.
Transpiration and the transpiration stream

Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from a plant, which diffuses out of the leaves through the stomata. The transpiration stream is the movement of water taken up by the roots and carried up through the xylem to the stems and leaves that replaces it.
Root hair cell
A cell on the outside of a root, drawn out into a long thin hair that gives a large surface area. It is adapted for the efficient uptake of water by osmosis and of mineral ions by active transport.
Stomata and guard cells
A stoma is a pore in the epidermis of a leaf. Each stoma is surrounded by a pair of guard cells that open and close it. The role of stomata and guard cells is to control gas exchange and water loss.
Plant organ system for transport
The roots, stem and leaves, which work together as an organ system for the transport of substances around the plant.

chemistry-structure-and-bonding-of-carbo.d: Chemistry — Structure and bonding of carbon
terms: Diamond

A form of carbon in which each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms in a giant covalent structure. Diamond is very hard, has a very high melting point and does not conduct electricity.
Giant covalent structure
A structure in which very many atoms are joined to one another by covalent bonds in a continuous network, so that there are no separate molecules. Diamond and graphite are giant covalent structures.
Covalent bond
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms. Covalent bonds are strong, so a great deal of energy is needed to break the many covalent bonds in a giant covalent structure.
Graphite
A form of carbon in which each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds with three other carbon atoms, forming layers of hexagonal rings which have no covalent bonds between the layers.
Hexagonal ring
A ring of six carbon atoms. The layers in graphite, and the sheet in graphene, are built from hexagonal rings of carbon atoms.
Delocalised electron
An electron that is not held in a bond between two particular atoms and is free to move through the structure. In graphite, one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised.
Graphene
A single layer of graphite. Its properties make it useful in electronics and composites.
Fullerene
A molecule of carbon atoms with a hollow shape. The structure of fullerenes is based on hexagonal rings of carbon atoms but they may also contain rings with five or seven carbon atoms.
Buckminsterfullerene
The first fullerene to be discovered, C₆₀, which has a spherical shape.
Carbon nanotube
A cylindrical fullerene with a very high length to diameter ratio. Carbon nanotubes are useful for nanotechnology, electronics and materials.
Length to diameter ratio
How many times longer a shape is than it is wide. Carbon nanotubes have very high length to diameter ratios: they are extremely long compared with how narrow they are.
Composite
A material made by combining two materials so that the mixture has properties neither has alone. Graphene and carbon nanotubes are added to composites to strengthen them.
Alternating potential difference (ac)
A potential difference that repeatedly changes direction, so the current it drives repeatedly reverses direction round the circuit. Mains electricity is an ac supply.
Direct potential difference (dc)
A potential difference that is always in the same direction, so the current it drives passes round the circuit in one direction only. Cells and batteries supply a direct potential difference.
UK domestic mains supply
The ac supply delivered to homes in the United Kingdom: a frequency of 50 Hz and a potential difference of about 230 V.
Frequency
The number of complete cycles of an alternating supply each second, measured in hertz (Hz). A 50 Hz supply completes 50 cycles every second.
Three-core cable
The cable used to connect most electrical appliances to the mains. It contains three wires: live, neutral and earth.
Live wire
The brown wire, which carries the alternating potential difference from the supply. It is at about 230 V relative to earth.
Neutral wire
The blue wire, which completes the circuit. It is at, or close to, earth potential (0 V).
Earth wire
