The green and yellow striped wire. It is a safety wire, at 0 V, which stops the appliance becoming live; it only carries a current if there is a fault.
Earth potential (0 V)
The potential of the ground, taken as 0 V. The potential difference between the live wire and earth is about 230 V, which is why any connection from live to earth is dangerous.
Colour coding of insulation
The insulation covering each wire is colour coded for easy identification: live wire brown, neutral wire blue, earth wire green and yellow stripes.
Becoming live
What happens when a fault lets the live wire touch the metal case of an appliance, raising the case to about 230 V. The earth wire is there to stop this.
Live-to-earth connection
Any path joining the live wire to earth, including a person touching the live wire while in contact with the ground. A large current passes along it because there is about 230 V across it.
Everyday electrical appliance
An everyday electrical appliance such as a kettle, a lamp or a food mixer is designed to bring about a particular energy transfer when a current flows through it.
Energy transferred by an appliance
The amount of energy an appliance transfers depends on two things: how long the appliance is switched on for, and the power of the appliance.
Appliances with electric motors
In appliances such as a food mixer, a drill or a washing machine, energy is transferred electrically from batteries or the ac mains to the kinetic energy of an electric motor.
Appliances with heating devices
In appliances such as a kettle, a toaster or an iron, energy is transferred electrically from the ac mains to a heating device, raising the temperature of water, food or metal.
Batteries and ac mains
Portable appliances are usually supplied by batteries, which provide a direct current. Appliances plugged into sockets are supplied by the ac mains.
Work done by flowing charge
Work is done when charge flows in a circuit. The energy transferred by that work comes from the store associated with the source, such as the chemical store of a battery.
energy transferred = power x time
The energy transferred by electrical work can be calculated from the power of the device and the time for which it operates: energy transferred = power x time.
E = P t
The symbol form of energy transferred = power x time, where E is energy transferred in joules, P is power in watts and t is time in seconds.
energy transferred = charge flow x potential difference
The energy transferred by electrical work can also be calculated from the charge that flows and the potential difference it moves through: energy transferred = charge flow x potential difference.
E = Q V
The symbol form of energy transferred = charge flow x potential difference, where E is energy transferred in joules, Q is charge flow in coulombs and V is potential difference in volts.
The joule
Energy transferred, E, is measured in joules, J. One joule is transferred when a power of one watt operates for one second.
The second
Time, t, is measured in seconds, s, in E = P t. Times given in minutes or hours must be converted to seconds before the equation is used.
The coulomb
Charge flow, Q, is measured in coulombs, C. A charge flow of one coulomb passes when a current of one ampere flows for one second.
Energy transferred over a given time

Because energy transferred = power x time, the power of a device is the energy it transfers divided by the time in seconds. Two devices can transfer the same energy at different powers if they run for different times.
Power rating of an appliance

The power rating printed on an appliance is the power it transfers when working normally. A higher power rating means a faster change in the stored energy of the appliance and its surroundings while it is in use.
The National Grid
The National Grid is a system of cables and transformers that links power stations to consumers such as homes, schools and factories.
Step-up transformer
A step-up transformer increases the potential difference from the power station to the transmission cables, which reduces the current in those cables for the same power.
Step-down transformer
A step-down transformer decreases the potential difference, to a much lower value, for domestic use, so that mains electricity reaches consumers at a safe potential difference.
Efficient transmission
Transmitting at a high potential difference means a low current in the cables. Because the power wasted by heating the cables is given by P = I^2 R, a lower current wastes much less energy.
pathogen
A microorganism that causes infectious disease. Pathogens may be viruses, bacteria, protists or fungi. They may infect plants or animals and can be spread by direct contact, by water or by air.
rapid reproduction of pathogens in the body
Bacteria and viruses may reproduce rapidly inside the body, so the number of pathogens present can rise quickly after an infection begins.
toxin
A poison that bacteria may produce. Toxins damage tissues and make us feel ill.
cell damage by viruses
Viruses live and reproduce inside cells, causing cell damage. This is how a viral infection harms the body, rather than by producing toxins.
salmonella food poisoning

A bacterial disease spread by bacteria ingested in food, or on food prepared in unhygienic conditions. Fever, abdominal cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea are caused by the bacteria and the toxins they secrete. In the UK, poultry are vaccinated against salmonella to control the spread.
gonorrhoea

A sexually transmitted disease (STD) caused by a bacterium, with symptoms of a thick yellow or green discharge from the vagina or penis and pain on urinating. It is spread by sexual contact. It was easily treated with the antibiotic penicillin until many resistant strains appeared. The spread can be controlled by treatment with antibiotics or the use of a barrier method of contraception such as a condom.
rose black spot

A fungal disease where purple or black spots develop on leaves, which often turn yellow and drop early. It affects the growth of the plant as photosynthesis is reduced. It is spread in the environment by water or wind, and can be treated by using fungicides and/or removing and destroying the affected leaves.
malarial protist
The pathogens that cause malaria are protists. Malaria causes recurrent episodes of fever and can be fatal.
vector

An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another without being the pathogen itself. The malarial protist has a life cycle that includes the mosquito, so the spread of malaria is controlled by preventing the vectors, mosquitos, from breeding and by using mosquito nets to avoid being bitten.
non-specific defence systems of the human body

Defences that act against pathogens in general rather than one particular pathogen: the skin acts as a barrier; the nose has hairs and mucus that trap particles from the air; the trachea and bronchi produce mucus that traps pathogens and have cilia that waft the mucus away from the lungs; the stomach produces hydrochloric acid that kills pathogens in swallowed food and mucus.
immune system
The body system that tries to destroy a pathogen if that pathogen enters the body, after the non-specific defences have been passed.
phagocytosis
One of the ways white blood cells help to defend against pathogens: the white blood cell takes the pathogen into itself and digests it.
antibody production

One of the ways white blood cells help to defend against pathogens: white blood cells produce antibodies against the pathogen. If the same pathogen re-enters the body the white blood cells respond quickly to produce the correct antibodies.
antitoxin production
One of the ways white blood cells help to defend against pathogens: white blood cells produce antitoxins, which counteract the toxins produced by bacteria.
vaccination

Introducing small quantities of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body to stimulate the white blood cells to produce antibodies. If the same pathogen re-enters the body the white blood cells respond quickly to produce the correct antibodies, preventing infection.
immunising a large proportion of the population
Vaccinating a large proportion of a population reduces the spread of a pathogen, because there are far fewer people the pathogen can infect and pass through.
antibiotic

A medicine, such as penicillin, that helps to cure bacterial disease by killing infective bacteria inside the body. It is important that specific bacteria should be treated by specific antibiotics. Antibiotics cannot kill viral pathogens.
antibiotic-resistant strain

A strain of bacteria that is not killed by an antibiotic. The use of antibiotics has greatly reduced deaths from infectious bacterial diseases, but the emergence of strains resistant to antibiotics is of great concern.
traditional sources of drugs

Traditionally drugs were extracted from plants and microorganisms. The heart drug digitalis originates from foxgloves. The painkiller aspirin originates from willow. Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming from the Penicillium mould.
toxicity, efficacy and dose
The three things for which new drugs are extensively tested: toxicity, which is how harmful the drug is; efficacy, which is how well it works; and dose, which is how much of it should be given.
preclinical testing
The stage of drug development done in a laboratory using cells, tissues and live animals, before the drug is given to people.
clinical trial

The stage of drug development that uses healthy volunteers and patients. Very low doses of the drug are given at the start of the clinical trial. If the drug is found to be safe, further clinical trials are carried out to find the optimum dose for the drug. In double blind trials, some patients are given a placebo.

chemistry-chemical-measurements-conserva.d: Chemistry — Chemical measurements, conservation of mass and the quantitative interpretation of chemical equations
terms: Law of conservation of mass
The law of conservation of mass states that no atoms are lost or made during a chemical reaction so the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants.
Symbol equation
A representation of a reaction using chemical formulae, with the reactants on the left of the arrow and the products on the right.
Balanced equation
A symbol equation in which the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides of the equation, which is what conservation of mass requires.
Multiplier in normal script
A number written in normal script before a formula, which multiplies every atom in that whole formula. In 2Ca(NO3)2 the leading 2 doubles the entire formula unit.
Subscript within a formula
A small number written after a symbol, or after a closing bracket, which multiplies only the atom or the bracketed group that it immediately follows.
Relative atomic mass (Ar)
The relative mass of an atom of an element, the building block from which a relative formula mass is assembled.
Relative formula mass (Mr)
The relative formula mass (Mr) of a compound is the sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the numbers shown in the formula.
Mass balance across an equation
In a balanced chemical equation the sum of the relative formula masses of the reactants in the quantities shown equals the sum of the relative formula masses of the products in the quantities shown.
Percentage by mass
The share of a compound's relative formula mass contributed by one element: the Ar of that element multiplied by the number of its atoms, divided by the Mr of the compound, then multiplied by 100.
Non-enclosed system
A reaction vessel open to the surroundings, so a gaseous reactant can enter or a gaseous product can leave without being weighed on the balance.
Thermal decomposition of a metal carbonate
Heating breaks the carbonate down into the metal oxide and carbon dioxide; the carbon dioxide escapes into the atmosphere, leaving the metal oxide as the only solid product.
Particle model explanation of a mass change
An account of an apparent mass change in terms of gas particles entering the vessel from the air, or leaving it and dispersing among the particles of the air.
Uncertainty
The doubt that always exists about the result of a measurement, present whenever a measurement is made, however good the apparatus and the technique.
Distribution of results
The pattern formed by a set of repeated measurements, showing where the results cluster and which of them lie apart from the rest.
Anomalous result
A measurement lying well outside the cluster formed by the others; it is spotted when the distribution is represented and is excluded from the mean.
Range as a measure of uncertainty
The difference between the largest and the smallest of a set of measurements, used about the mean as a measure of uncertainty and quoted as the mean plus or minus half the range.

physics-changes-of-state-and-the-particl.d: Physics — Changes of state and the particle model
terms: Density

Density is how much mass a material packs into each unit of volume. Because it is a ratio, it belongs to the material rather than to the lump of material: a small piece and a large piece of the same metal at the same temperature have the same density.
The density equation
The specification defines density by density = mass / volume. Mass goes on the top and volume on the bottom, so for a fixed mass a larger volume always means a smaller density.
The symbols in the equation

In the symbol form of the equation, written as rho = m/V, rho stands for density, m stands for mass and V stands for volume. The symbols are not initials of the words, which is why they have to be learned.
The unit of density
The specification gives density, rho, in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m^3. The unit follows straight from the equation: a mass in kilograms divided by a volume in metres cubed.
Mass in the density equation
Mass, m, is measured in kilograms, kg. A balance usually reads in grams, so a reading in grams must be divided by 1000 before it is used to obtain a density in kg/m^3.
Volume in the density equation
Volume, V, is measured in metres cubed, m^3. For a regular solid the volume is found by multiplying length by width by height. A volume in cm^3 must be divided by 1 000 000 to convert it to m^3.
Converting g/cm^3 to kg/m^3
One gram per centimetre cubed is one thousand kilograms per metre cubed, so a density in g/cm^3 is multiplied by 1000 to give kg/m^3. Water is 1.0 g/cm^3, which is 1000 kg/m^3.
The particle model

The particle model pictures a substance as a very large number of tiny particles in constant motion. Their spacing and arrangement explain both the three states of matter and the differences in density between those states.
Particle model of a solid
In a solid the particles are packed closely together in a fixed, regular arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions. A solid therefore keeps its own shape and has a fixed volume.
Particle model of a liquid

In a liquid the particles are still close together and touching, but the arrangement is random and the particles can move past one another. A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container.
Particle model of a gas
In a gas the particles are far apart, arranged randomly and moving quickly in all directions. A gas has no fixed shape or volume and fills whatever container it is put in.
Simple particle diagrams

A simple diagram uses identical circles for the particles. A solid is drawn as circles touching in a regular pattern, a liquid as circles touching in a random pattern, and a gas as widely separated circles. The circles are the same size in all three diagrams.
Explaining density differences

For the same substance the particles have the same mass in every state, so density depends only on how closely they are packed. Solids and liquids have similar, high densities; a gas has a much lower density because the same particles are spread through a far larger volume.
Density of a regular solid

For a regularly shaped object the mass is found on a balance and the volume is calculated from measured dimensions, for example length x width x height for a cuboid. Density is then the mass divided by that volume.
Displacement technique

For an irregularly shaped object the volume is found by lowering it into a measuring cylinder of water, or into a displacement can, and recording the volume of water pushed out of the way. The volume of the object is the rise in level, that is the final reading minus the starting reading.
Density of a liquid

The mass of the empty measuring cylinder is recorded, a measured volume of liquid is poured in, and the cylinder is weighed again. The mass of the liquid is the difference between the two readings, and that mass is divided by the measured volume.
Choosing measuring apparatus

A ruler is suitable for lengths of a few centimetres, Vernier callipers resolve to about 0.1 mm and suit small objects, and a micrometer resolves to about 0.01 mm and suits thin wires and sheets. The instrument is chosen so that its resolution is small compared with the length being measured.
Changes of state
Melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing and subliming are changes of state. The particles gain or lose energy and rearrange, but no particles are created or destroyed.
Conservation of mass in a change of state

When a substance changes state the number of particles and the mass of each particle are unchanged, so the total mass is unchanged. A balance reading only falls because gas has escaped from the container, not because mass has vanished.
Physical change

A change of state is a physical change: no new substance is made, and reversing the change returns the material to its original properties. In a chemical change new substances are formed and the original properties are not recovered by simply reversing the conditions.

chemistry-use-of-amount-of-substance-in-.d: Chemistry — Use of amount of substance in relation to masses of pure substances
terms: Mole (mol)
The unit in which chemical amounts are measured; the symbol for the unit mole is mol. A label such as '0.50 mol of sodium chloride' states a chemical amount, not a mass and not a volume.
Mass of one mole
The mass of one mole of a substance in grams is numerically equal to its relative formula mass. One mole of CaCO₃ (Mr = 100) has a mass of 100 g; one mole of H₂O (Mr = 18) has a mass of 18 g.
Equal amounts, equal numbers of particles

One mole of a substance contains the same number of the stated particles - atoms, molecules or ions - as one mole of any other substance. Equal amounts in moles therefore mean equal numbers of particles, however different the masses are.
Avogadro constant
The number of atoms, molecules or ions in a mole of a given substance. Its value is 6.02 x 10²³ per mole. It is a number of particles per mole, not per gram.
Amounts of different particles

Amounts in moles can be applied to atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, formulae and equations. In one mole of carbon (C) the number of atoms is the same as the number of molecules in one mole of carbon dioxide (CO₂), although one mole of CO₂ contains three moles of atoms.
Moles from mass
The number of moles in a given mass is found by dividing that mass in grams by the relative formula mass: number of moles = mass ÷ Mr. 20 g of CaCO₃ (Mr = 100) is 0.20 mol.
Mass from moles
The mass of a known amount is found by multiplying the amount in moles by the relative formula mass: mass = number of moles x Mr. 0.25 mol of MgCl₂ (Mr = 95) has a mass of 23.75 g.
Masses from a balanced equation
The masses of reactants and products can be calculated from balanced symbol equations. In a closed system the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants that reacted.
Reading an equation in moles

Chemical equations can be interpreted in terms of moles. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ shows that one mole of magnesium reacts with two moles of hydrochloric acid to produce one mole of magnesium chloride and one mole of hydrogen gas.
Mole ratio

The balancing numbers in an equation give the ratio of the amounts in moles of the substances involved. They do not give the ratio of the masses, because each substance has its own relative formula mass.
Reacting mass calculation

To find the mass of one substance from the mass of another: convert the known mass to moles using its Mr, apply the mole ratio from the balanced equation, then convert back to a mass using the Mr of the substance wanted.
Balancing numbers from masses

The balancing numbers in a symbol equation can be calculated from the masses of reactants and products by converting the masses in grams to amounts in moles and converting the numbers of moles to simple whole number ratios.
Simple whole number ratio

The amounts in moles are divided through by the smallest of them, and multiplied up if needed, so that the balancing numbers are the simplest whole numbers that fit. 0.2 : 0.1 : 0.2 becomes 2 : 1 : 2.
Changing the subject
A relationship can be rearranged to make any of its quantities the subject. From number of moles = mass ÷ Mr come mass = number of moles x Mr and Mr = mass ÷ number of moles.
Excess reactant
A reactant supplied in more than the amount the equation requires. Using an excess of one reactant makes sure that all of the other reactant is used up.
Limiting reactant

The reactant that is completely used up in a reaction. It is called the limiting reactant because it limits the amount of products: the amount of product is worked out from the amount of the limiting reactant, not from the reactant in excess.

physics-internal-energy-and-energy-trans.d: Physics — Internal energy and energy transfers
terms: Internal energy
The energy stored inside a system by the particles (atoms and molecules) that make up that system. It is a store held by the particles, not a fluid that enters or leaves the system.
Kinetic energy of particles
The energy the particles have because they are moving, vibrating or rotating. It is one of the two contributions to internal energy, and it is the contribution linked to temperature.
Potential energy of particles

The energy stored because of the positions of the particles relative to one another and the forces between them. It is the second contribution to internal energy, and it is the store that changes during a change of state.
Heating
An energy transfer that increases the energy of the particles that make up a system. The result is either a rise in the temperature of the system or a change of state.
Change in thermal energy equation
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change, written in symbols as ∆E = m c ∆θ. It applies when heating or cooling changes the temperature of a substance.
Quantities in ∆E = m c ∆θ
Change in thermal energy, ∆E, is in joules, J; mass, m, is in kilograms, kg; temperature change, ∆θ, is in degrees Celsius, °C.
Units of specific heat capacity
Specific heat capacity, c, is measured in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/kg °C, because it is an energy quoted for each kilogram and for each degree Celsius of temperature change.
Specific heat capacity
The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius.
Change of state
A change between solid, liquid and vapour in which the substance stays the same substance. While it happens the temperature does not change, even though energy is still being transferred.
Latent heat
The energy needed for a substance to change state. It changes the energy stored (internal energy) of the substance but not its temperature.
Specific latent heat
The amount of energy required to change the state of one kilogram of a substance with no change in temperature. Energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat, or E = m L.
Quantities in E = m L
Energy, E, is in joules, J; mass, m, is in kilograms, kg; specific latent heat, L, is in joules per kilogram, J/kg. No temperature unit appears because the temperature does not change.
Specific latent heat of fusion
The specific latent heat for the change of state from solid to liquid, that is for melting, and in reverse for freezing.
Specific latent heat of vaporisation
The specific latent heat for the change of state from liquid to vapour, that is for boiling, and in reverse for condensing.
Heating and cooling graph

A graph of temperature against time for a substance heated or cooled at a steady rate. Sloping sections show the temperature changing within one state; flat sections show a change of state, where energy is still transferred but the temperature is constant.
Constant random motion

The molecules of a gas are in constant random motion. They travel in all directions and at a wide range of speeds, changing direction whenever they collide with each other or with the walls of the container. No molecule keeps one path or one speed for long.
Temperature and average kinetic energy

The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its molecules. Raising the temperature raises that average, so the molecules move faster on average. Individual molecules still have a range of speeds; temperature describes the average, not any one molecule.
Gas pressure

Gas pressure arises from the collisions of the moving gas molecules with the walls of the container. Each collision exerts a small force on the wall; the huge number of collisions every second adds up to a steady net force spread over the wall area.
Constant volume

A gas is at constant volume when it is sealed in a rigid container that cannot expand or contract, so the space the gas occupies cannot change. Only the temperature and the pressure are free to change.
Pressure and temperature at constant volume

Changing the temperature of a gas held at constant volume changes the pressure it exerts. Heating raises the average kinetic energy, so the molecules hit the walls more frequently and with more force, and the pressure rises. Cooling has the opposite effect.
photosynthesis

The reaction represented by the equation carbon dioxide + water → (light) glucose + oxygen, which takes place in the chloroplasts. Written with chemical symbols, CO2 and H2O react to form C6H12O6 and O2.
endothermic reaction
A reaction that takes in energy from its surroundings. Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction in which energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light.
rate of photosynthesis
The amount of product formed in a given time, calculated by dividing the amount of product by the time taken, for example bubbles of oxygen released per minute or cm3 of oxygen produced per minute.
limiting factor

The factor that is controlling the rate of photosynthesis at that moment, so that increasing it increases the rate. Temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and the amount of chlorophyll all affect the rate of photosynthesis.
interaction of limiting factors

Temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and the amount of chlorophyll interact, and any one of them may be the factor that limits photosynthesis. On a graph, the limiting factor is the one which, when increased on its own, raises the rate further.
inverse square law and light intensity

Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source. Doubling the distance reduces the light intensity to one quarter, and halving the distance increases it four times.
limiting factors in greenhouses

Growers enhance temperature, light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration in greenhouses to gain the maximum rate of photosynthesis. The cost of enhancing the conditions must be less than the extra income gained, so limiting factors are important in the economics of greenhouse growing.
uses of glucose

The glucose produced in photosynthesis may be used for respiration, converted into insoluble starch for storage, used to produce fat or oil for storage, used to produce cellulose which strengthens the cell wall, or used to produce amino acids for protein synthesis.
nitrate ions
Ions that are absorbed from the soil and used by plants, together with the glucose produced in photosynthesis, to produce amino acids for protein synthesis.
effect of carbon dioxide concentration

Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis, so its concentration affects the rate. While carbon dioxide is the limiting factor, increasing its concentration increases the rate; once another factor becomes limiting, the rate levels off.
amount of chlorophyll

Chlorophyll absorbs the light used in photosynthesis, so the amount of chlorophyll affects the rate. A shortage of chlorophyll, for example in the white areas of a variegated leaf or in a magnesium-deficient plant, lowers the rate because less light is absorbed.
source of plant biomass

The extra mass a plant gains as it grows comes mainly from carbon dioxide taken in from the air and fixed during photosynthesis to make glucose. Water is also a raw material, while the soil supplies only small amounts of mineral ions, not the bulk of the mass.
Oxidation (in terms of oxygen)
A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen. When a metal reacts with oxygen the metal gains oxygen, so the metal is oxidised.
Reduction (in terms of oxygen)
A reaction in which a substance loses oxygen. When a metal oxide is heated with carbon the oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced.
Metal oxide
The compound formed when a metal reacts with oxygen, for example magnesium oxide from magnesium burning in air.
Redox reaction
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction happen together: oxygen lost by one substance is gained by another.
Reactivity series
A list of metals arranged in order of their reactivity, deduced from their reactions with water and with dilute acids.
Tendency to form positive ions
The readiness with which a metal atom loses its outer electrons to become a positive ion. The greater this tendency, the more reactive the metal.
Displacement reaction
A reaction in which a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in a compound.
Carbon and hydrogen in the series
The two non-metals often included in the reactivity series as reference points; carbon sits between magnesium and zinc, hydrogen between iron and copper.
Reaction of a metal with water
A reaction at room temperature giving a metal hydroxide and hydrogen, shown by potassium, sodium, lithium and calcium, and only very slowly by magnesium.
Reaction of a metal with dilute acid
A reaction giving a salt and hydrogen, shown by magnesium, zinc and iron; copper does not react with dilute acid.
Native metal
A metal found in the Earth as the element itself rather than as a compound, because it is very unreactive; gold is the standard example.
Ore
A rock containing enough of a metal compound to make extracting the metal worthwhile.
Extraction by reduction with carbon
Heating the oxide of a metal that is less reactive than carbon with carbon, so that the carbon takes the oxygen and the metal is left.
Oxidation (in terms of electrons)
The loss of electrons by a species during a reaction.
Reduction (in terms of electrons)
The gain of electrons by a species during a reaction.
Ionic equation
An equation showing only the species that change in a reaction, with spectator ions left out.
Half equation
An equation showing the electrons lost or gained by one species, for example Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu.
Spectator ion
An ion present in the reaction mixture that is unchanged by the reaction and is therefore omitted from the ionic equation.
Atom
The smallest particle of an element that still behaves as that element. Atoms are very small, having a radius of about 1 x 10^-10 metres.
Nucleus

The tiny positively charged centre of an atom, composed of both protons and neutrons. Its radius is less than 1/10 000 of the radius of the atom, yet most of the mass of the atom is concentrated in it.
Proton
A positively charged particle found in the nucleus. Every nucleus of a given element contains the same number of protons.
Neutron
An uncharged particle found in the nucleus alongside the protons. Changing the number of neutrons gives a different isotope of the same element.
Electron
A negatively charged particle arranged at different distances from the nucleus, outside it. In an atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
Scale of the nucleus
The nucleus is less than one ten-thousandth of the atomic radius, so on a scale drawing of an atom the nucleus would be invisible and the atom is mostly empty space.
Energy level
One of the different distances from the nucleus at which electrons in an atom are arranged. Electrons further from the nucleus are at higher energy levels.
Absorption of electromagnetic radiation
When an atom absorbs electromagnetic radiation an electron may move further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level.
Emission of electromagnetic radiation
When an electron moves closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level, the atom emits electromagnetic radiation.
Electrical neutrality
An atom has no overall electrical charge because the number of negative electrons equals the number of positive protons in the nucleus.
Atomic number
The number of protons in an atom of an element. All atoms of a particular element have the same atomic number.
Mass number
The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom.
Nuclear symbol
The conventional representation of an atom, with the mass number written above the atomic number to the left of the chemical symbol, for example mass number 23 and atomic number 11 for sodium.
Isotope
One of two or more atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, and therefore different mass numbers.
Positive ion
An atom that has lost one or more outer electrons, so that protons outnumber electrons and the particle carries a positive charge.
Scientific model
A description or picture used to explain observations. New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.
Indivisible sphere model
The idea, held before the discovery of the electron, that atoms were tiny spheres that could not be divided.
Plum pudding model
The model that followed the discovery of the electron: the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
Alpha particle scattering experiment
The experiment whose results led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom was concentrated at the centre and that the nucleus was charged.
Nuclear model
The model in which the mass and the charge of an atom are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus, with electrons outside it. It replaced the plum pudding model.
Bohr model
Niels Bohr's adaptation of the nuclear model, in which electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances. His theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations.
Discovery of the proton

Later experiments led to the idea that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each with the same amount of positive charge; these were named protons.
Chadwick's evidence
The experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence for neutrons within the nucleus, about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted scientific idea.
Cellular respiration
An exothermic reaction which is continuously occurring in living cells, transferring energy from glucose. The energy transferred supplies all the energy needed for living processes.
Exothermic reaction
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings. Because respiration is exothermic, respiring cells and tissues get warmer as energy is transferred.
Uses of the energy transferred by respiration

Organisms need energy for chemical reactions to build larger molecules, for movement, and for keeping warm. The energy transferred is also used for the continual enzyme controlled processes of metabolism that synthesise new molecules.
Aerobic respiration
Respiration in cells that takes place using oxygen. Glucose is completely oxidised, so a relatively large amount of energy is transferred compared with anaerobic respiration.
Anaerobic respiration
Respiration in cells that takes place without oxygen, to transfer energy. The products differ from those of aerobic respiration and much less energy is transferred.
Equation for aerobic respiration
Aerobic respiration is represented by the equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
Chemical symbols in respiration
C6H12O6 is glucose, O2 is oxygen, CO2 is carbon dioxide and H2O is water. These symbols are used in place of the words in the equation for aerobic respiration.
Anaerobic respiration in muscles
Anaerobic respiration in muscles is represented by the equation: glucose → lactic acid. No carbon dioxide or water is produced by this reaction.
Incomplete oxidation of glucose
In anaerobic respiration the oxidation of glucose is incomplete, so much less energy is transferred than in aerobic respiration.
Anaerobic respiration in plant and yeast cells
Anaerobic respiration in plant and yeast cells is represented by the equation: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide.
Fermentation

Anaerobic respiration in yeast cells. It has economic importance in the manufacture of bread, where the carbon dioxide makes the dough rise, and of alcoholic drinks, which contain the ethanol produced.
Response of the body to exercise
During exercise the human body reacts to the increased demand for energy. The heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume increase during exercise to supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood.
Muscle fatigue and oxygen debt in exercise

If insufficient oxygen is supplied, anaerobic respiration takes place in muscles. The incomplete oxidation of glucose causes a build up of lactic acid and creates an oxygen debt. During long periods of vigorous activity muscles become fatigued and stop contracting efficiently.
Oxygen debt and the fate of lactic acid

Blood flowing through the muscles transports the lactic acid to the liver, where it is converted back into glucose. Oxygen debt is the amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells.
Metabolism

The sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body. The energy transferred by respiration in cells is used by the organism for these continual enzyme controlled processes, which synthesise new molecules.
Reactions included in metabolism

Metabolism includes: conversion of glucose to starch, glycogen and cellulose; the formation of lipid molecules from a molecule of glycerol and three molecules of fatty acids; the use of glucose and nitrate ions to form amino acids which in turn are used to synthesise proteins; respiration; and the breakdown of excess proteins to form urea for excretion.
Small molecules used in synthesis and breakdown

Sugars are used to synthesise carbohydrates such as starch, glycogen and cellulose; amino acids are used to synthesise proteins, and excess protein is broken down to form urea; glycerol and fatty acids are used to synthesise lipids. Breakdown of these larger molecules releases the same small molecules again.
Salt

A compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal ion or by another positive ion. The acid supplies the negative ion and the metal, base, alkali or carbonate supplies the positive ion.
Acid + metal reaction
Acids react with some metals to produce a salt and hydrogen: for example Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. The hydrogen is seen as bubbles of gas.
'Some metals'
Only metals more reactive than hydrogen release hydrogen from a dilute acid. Magnesium, zinc and iron do; copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid.
Oxidation
Loss of electrons. When a metal reacts with an acid the metal atoms lose electrons to form positive ions, so the metal is oxidised.
Reduction
Gain of electrons. In an acid-metal reaction the hydrogen ions gain electrons to become hydrogen molecules, so they are reduced.
Redox reaction
A reaction in which electrons are transferred, so that oxidation and reduction happen together. Acid-metal reactions are redox reactions.
Half equation
An equation showing the electrons lost or gained by one species, such as Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ or 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.
Spectator ion
An ion that is present but unchanged by the reaction, such as the chloride ion when magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid.
Base
A substance that neutralises an acid to give a salt and water. Insoluble metal hydroxides and metal oxides are bases.
Alkali
A base that dissolves in water, such as a soluble metal hydroxide. Its aqueous solution contains hydroxide ions.
Neutralisation
The reaction of an acid with a base, alkali or carbonate in which the acid is used up and a salt is formed.
Acid + carbonate reaction
Metal carbonates neutralise acids to produce a salt, water and carbon dioxide, which is why the mixture fizzes.
Naming a salt
The salt's name has two parts: the first comes from the positive ion of the base, alkali or carbonate, the second from the acid used.
Salt families
Hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, nitric acid produces nitrates and sulfuric acid produces sulfates.
Source of the positive ion
The positive ion in a salt comes from the base, alkali or carbonate, not from the acid and not from the water formed.
Predicting products
Acid + metal gives salt + hydrogen; acid + base or alkali gives salt + water; acid + carbonate gives salt + water + carbon dioxide.
Common ions
Familiar ions used to build salt formulae include Na⁺, K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺, Cl⁻, NO₃⁻, SO₄²⁻ and CO₃²⁻.
Balancing charges in a formula
A salt formula is neutral overall, so the ions are combined in the ratio that cancels the charges, using brackets where a whole ion is repeated, as in Ca(NO₃)₂.
Soluble salt preparation
A soluble salt is made by reacting an acid with a solid insoluble metal, metal oxide, hydroxide or carbonate, then removing the unreacted solid.
Excess solid
Solid is added until no more reacts, which guarantees that all the acid has been used and none is left to contaminate the salt.
Filtration
Separating an insoluble solid from a liquid using filter paper. The unreacted solid stays as the residue; the dissolved salt passes through as the filtrate.
Crystallisation
Concentrating a salt solution by evaporating some of the water and then leaving it, so that crystals of the solid salt form as the rest evaporates.
Pure, dry sample
Crystals that contain no unreacted acid or solid and no remaining water; they are patted dry between filter papers rather than heated hard.
Required practical 1
Preparation of a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt from an insoluble oxide or carbonate, using a Bunsen burner to heat the dilute acid.
Water bath or electric heater
The gentle heating used to evaporate the salt solution in Required practical 1, so that the salt is not decomposed and crystals can form.
Hydrogen ion, H⁺
The ion that all acids produce in aqueous solution; it is what makes a solution acidic.
Hydroxide ion, OH⁻
The ion present in aqueous solutions of alkalis; it is what makes a solution alkaline.
pH scale
A scale from 0 to 14 measuring the acidity or alkalinity of a solution, measured with universal indicator or a pH probe.
pH probe
An instrument that gives a numerical pH reading directly, more precisely than a colour chart can.
Neutral solution
A solution with pH 7. Below 7 a solution is acidic, above 7 it is alkaline.
Neutralisation in ionic terms
In neutralisation between an acid and an alkali, the hydrogen ions from the acid react with the hydroxide ions from the alkali to produce water.
Ionic equation for neutralisation
H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, the equation the specification gives for the reaction of hydrogen ions with hydroxide ions.
Universal indicator
A wide range indicator whose colour is matched to a chart to give an approximate pH.
Reading the pH scale
A measured pH is used to classify a solution: below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 alkaline.
Strong acid
An acid that is completely ionised in aqueous solution. Hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric acids are strong acids.
Weak acid
An acid that is only partially ionised in aqueous solution. Ethanoic, citric and carbonic acids are weak acids.
Degree of ionisation
The fraction of the acid molecules that have released their hydrogen ions. It is what strong and weak describe.
Hydrogen ion concentration and pH
As pH falls by one unit the hydrogen ion concentration increases by a factor of 10.
Dilute
A small amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution. Dilute is about amount, not about ionisation.
Concentrated
A large amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution. A weak acid can still be concentrated.
Relative acidity
Comparing solutions by pH: the lower the whole-number pH, the greater the hydrogen ion concentration, with pH 7 as neutral.
Radioactive decay
The process in which an unstable nucleus gives out radiation as it changes to become more stable. It is a random process.
Unstable nucleus
A nucleus that will give out radiation at some point because its present combination of protons and neutrons is not stable.
Random process
A process in which it is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next, or when a particular nucleus will decay. Only the average behaviour of a large number of nuclei is predictable.
Activity
The rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays.
Becquerel (Bq)
The unit in which activity is measured. One becquerel is one decay each second.
Count-rate
The number of decays recorded each second by a detector. It is smaller than the activity of the source, because a detector only intercepts some of the radiation emitted.
Geiger-Muller tube
A detector of nuclear radiation. Each particle or ray it absorbs produces a pulse, and the pulses are counted to give a count-rate.
Nuclear radiation
The radiation emitted by an unstable nucleus. It may be an alpha particle, a beta particle, a gamma ray or a neutron.
Alpha particle (α)
A particle emitted from a nucleus consisting of two neutrons and two protons; it is the same as a helium nucleus.
Beta particle (β)
A high speed electron ejected from the nucleus as a neutron turns into a proton.
Gamma ray (γ)
Electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus.
Neutron emission (n)
The emission of a neutron from an unstable nucleus. It is one of the types of nuclear radiation listed by the specification.
Penetration through materials
How far radiation travels into a material before it is absorbed. Alpha is stopped by paper or skin, beta by a few millimetres of aluminium, and gamma is only reduced by thick lead or concrete.
Range in air
How far radiation travels through air before it is absorbed. Alpha travels a few centimetres, beta about a metre, and gamma travels a very long way.
Ionising power
How strongly radiation removes electrons from the atoms it passes. Alpha is the most ionising, beta is weaker, and gamma is the least ionising.
Nuclear equation
An equation used to represent radioactive decay, showing the parent nucleus on the left and the products of the decay on the right.
Mass number
The top number in a nuclear symbol, giving the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. It must balance across a nuclear equation.
Atomic number
The bottom number in a nuclear symbol, giving the number of protons and therefore the charge of the nucleus. It must balance across a nuclear equation.
Change caused by alpha decay
Alpha decay causes both the mass and the charge of the nucleus to decrease: the mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number falls by 2.
Change caused by beta decay
Beta decay does not cause the mass of the nucleus to change but does cause the charge of the nucleus to increase: the atomic number rises by 1.
Change caused by gamma emission
The emission of a gamma ray does not cause the mass or the charge of the nucleus to change.
Balancing a nuclear equation
Choosing the mass numbers and atomic numbers so that the total mass number and the total atomic number are the same on both sides of the equation.
Half-life
The time it takes for the number of nuclei of an isotope in a sample to halve, or the time it takes for the count rate or activity from the sample to fall to half its initial level.
Net decline as a ratio
After n half-lives the emission has fallen by a factor of 2 to the power n, so the net decline is written as the ratio 1 : 2 to the power n.
Radioactive contamination
The unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials. The hazard is due to the decay of the contaminating atoms.
Irradiation
The process of exposing an object to nuclear radiation. The irradiated object does not become radioactive.
Precautions against a source

Steps such as handling a source with tongs, keeping it at a distance, limiting exposure time and storing it in a lead-lined container, taken to protect against any hazard the source used for irradiation may present.
Peer review
The checking of published findings by other scientists. It is why studies of the effects of radiation on humans must be published and shared.
Choosing a source for a use

Selecting the radiation whose penetration, range in air and ionising power suit the job: alpha where the radiation must be absorbed over a short distance, beta where it must pass through thin material, gamma where it must pass through thick material or out of a body.
Symbol for an alpha particle
In a nuclear equation an alpha particle may be represented by the symbol ⁴₂He, with mass number 4 written above and atomic number 2 below.
Symbol for a beta particle
In a nuclear equation a beta particle is represented by the symbol ⁰₋₁e, with mass number 0 written above and charge −1 below.
Electrolyte
An ionic compound that has been melted or dissolved in water, so that its ions are free to move about within the liquid or solution. Electrolytes conduct electricity.
Electrolysis
The process in which passing an electric current through an electrolyte makes the ions move to the electrodes, where they are discharged to produce elements.
Cathode
The negative electrode. Positively charged ions move to it.
Anode
The positive electrode. Negatively charged ions move to it.
Inert electrode
An electrode, such as graphite or platinum, that does not take part in the reactions of the cell, so the products come only from the electrolyte.
Discharge
The loss of charge by an ion at an electrode, as electrons are gained or lost, turning the ion into a neutral atom or molecule of an element.
Binary ionic compound
An ionic compound made of just two elements, one metal and one non-metal, such as lead bromide or magnesium chloride.
Products of a molten binary compound
When a molten binary ionic compound is electrolysed with inert electrodes, the metal is produced at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode.
Extraction by electrolysis
Obtaining a metal from its molten compound by electrolysis. It is used when the metal is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon, or when the metal reacts with carbon.
Energy cost of extraction
Large amounts of energy are used in extraction by electrolysis, both to melt the compound and to produce the electrical current.
Cryolite
The compound mixed with aluminium oxide in the aluminium cell. The mixture melts at a lower temperature than aluminium oxide alone, so less energy is needed.
Aluminium cell anode
The positive electrode is made of carbon. Oxygen produced there reacts with the hot carbon, so the electrode is worn away and must be replaced continually.
Cathode rule in solution
At the negative electrode hydrogen is produced if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen; otherwise the metal is produced.
Anode rule in solution
At the positive electrode oxygen is produced unless the solution contains halide ions, when the halogen is produced.
Breakdown of water
In an aqueous solution water molecules break down producing hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions, and these ions can be discharged at the electrodes.
Hypothesis
A testable idea, put forward before the experiment, that predicts what will happen and can be supported or disproved by the results of Required practical 3.
Reduction
Gain of electrons. At the cathode positively charged ions gain electrons, so the reactions there are reductions.
Oxidation
Loss of electrons. At the anode negatively charged ions lose electrons, so the reactions there are oxidations.
Half equation
An equation showing the reaction at one electrode only, including the electrons gained or lost, balanced for both atoms and charge.
Cathode half equation example
2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
Anode half equation example
4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻, which may also be written as 4OH⁻ – 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O.
Test for hydrogen
A lit splint gives a squeaky pop with hydrogen. A glowing splint relights in oxygen, and damp litmus paper is bleached by chlorine.
homeostasis
The regulation of the internal conditions of a cell or organism to maintain optimum conditions for function, in response to internal and external changes.
receptor
A cell that detects a stimulus, which is a change in the environment.
coordination centre
A part of the body, such as the brain, spinal cord or pancreas, that receives and processes information from receptors.
effector
A muscle or gland that brings about a response which restores the optimum level.
internal conditions controlled in the human body
In the human body, the conditions controlled by homeostasis include blood glucose concentration, body temperature and water levels.
Conservation of energy in reactions

Energy is conserved in chemical reactions: the amount of energy in the universe at the end of a chemical reaction is the same as before the reaction takes place. Energy is only moved between the reacting chemicals and their surroundings.
Surroundings

Everything outside the reacting chemicals themselves, including the solvent, the container and the air. It is the temperature of the surroundings that a thermometer in the reaction mixture actually measures.
Exothermic reaction
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases. The product molecules end up with less energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred.
Endothermic reaction
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
Combustion
The reaction of a substance with oxygen, releasing energy. Combustion is exothermic.
Oxidation
A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen. Many oxidation reactions, such as the slow oxidation of iron in a hand warmer, are exothermic.
Neutralisation
The reaction of an acid with a base or alkali to form a salt and water. Neutralisation is exothermic.
Thermal decomposition
The breaking down of a compound into simpler substances on heating, for example calcium carbonate into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. Thermal decompositions are endothermic.
Self-heating can
An everyday use of an exothermic reaction: a reaction in a separate compartment of the can transfers energy to the drink and warms it.
Hand warmer
An everyday use of an exothermic reaction: iron powder oxidises slowly inside the pack and transfers energy to the surroundings.
Sports injury pack
A use of an endothermic reaction: the reaction inside the pack takes in energy from the surroundings, so the pack and the injury are cooled.
Temperature change of the surroundings
The rise or fall in temperature measured before and after a reaction. A rise shows an exothermic reaction; a fall shows an endothermic one.
Required practical 4
An investigation of the variables that affect temperature changes in reacting solutions, such as acid plus metals, acid plus carbonates, neutralisations and displacement of metals.
Collision
Chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy; a collision with too little energy does not lead to a reaction.
Activation energy
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react. It is the energy needed for a reaction to occur.
Reaction profile
An energy level diagram showing the relative energies of reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change, with a curved line showing the energy as the reaction proceeds.
Overall energy change
The difference in energy between the reactants and the products, shown on a reaction profile and, at higher tier, calculated from bond energies.
Bond breaking
Energy must be supplied to break bonds in the reactants, so bond breaking takes energy in.
Bond making
Energy is released when bonds in the products are formed.
Bond energy
The energy associated with a particular bond, used to calculate the energy needed to break bonds and the energy released when bonds are formed.
Scalar quantity
A quantity that has magnitude only. A scalar is fully described by a size and a unit, with no direction attached to it. Mass, speed, distance, energy and time are scalars.
Vector quantity
A quantity that has magnitude and an associated direction. A vector is only fully described when both are given. Force, weight, velocity, displacement and acceleration are vectors.
Vector arrow

The representation of a vector quantity by an arrow drawn on a diagram. The length of the arrow represents the magnitude of the vector, and the direction the arrow points represents the direction of the vector quantity.
Force

A push or pull that acts on an object due to the interaction with another object. A force is not something an object stores or owns; it exists only while two objects interact, and it is measured in newtons.
Contact force
A force between two objects that are physically touching. Friction, air resistance, tension and the normal contact force are contact forces.
Non-contact force
A force between two objects that are physically separated. Gravitational force, electrostatic force and magnetic force are non-contact forces.
Friction
A contact force that acts between two surfaces that are touching, acting along the surfaces and opposing the relative motion, or attempted motion, between them.
Air resistance
A contact force acting on an object moving through air. The object is physically touching the particles of the air, which is why it is classed as a contact force.
Tension
A contact force transmitted along a stretched rope, string, cable or spring, pulling on the objects attached at each end of it.
Normal contact force
The contact force exerted by a surface on an object that is touching it, acting at right angles (normal) to that surface.
Gravitational force
A non-contact force of attraction between two objects that have mass. It acts even though the objects are physically separated, for example between the Earth and an object above its surface.
Electrostatic force
A non-contact force between electrically charged objects. Like charges repel and opposite charges attract, and the force acts across the space between the charged objects.
Magnetic force
A non-contact force between magnets, or between a magnet and a magnetic material, which acts across the gap between them without the objects touching.
Interaction pair
The two forces produced when two objects interact. Each object exerts a force on the other, the two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, and each force acts on a different object.
Weight

The force acting on an object due to gravity, measured in newtons, N. Close to the Earth it is due to the gravitational field around the Earth, and it is calculated from weight = mass × gravitational field strength.
Gravitational field strength

The quantity, symbol g, measured in newtons per kilogram, N/kg, that describes the strength of a gravitational field at a point. The weight of an object depends on the gravitational field strength at the point where the object is.
Mass

The quantity of matter in an object, symbol m, measured in kilograms, kg. Mass is a scalar quantity and it does not change when the object is moved to a place with a different gravitational field strength.
Centre of mass

The single point at which the weight of an object may be considered to act. Treating the weight as one force acting at this point allows an object to be handled as though all of its mass were concentrated there.
Directly proportional

A relationship in which one quantity is a fixed multiple of another, so that multiplying one by a number multiplies the other by the same number, and a graph of one against the other is a straight line through the origin. The weight of an object and the mass of an object are directly proportional.
Newtonmeter
A calibrated spring-balance used to measure weight in newtons. The spring extends more as the force pulling on it increases, and the scale is marked so that the reading gives the weight directly.
Resultant force
The single force that has the same effect as all of the original forces acting on an object together. A number of forces acting on an object may always be replaced by this one force.
Free body diagram

A diagram showing a single isolated object or system on its own, with every force acting on that object drawn as an arrow from it. It is used to describe qualitatively how several forces combine to give a resultant force.
Balanced forces
Forces on an object that combine to give a resultant force of zero. The individual forces are still acting, but they have no overall effect on the motion of the object.
Resolving a force
Replacing a single force by two component forces acting at right angles to each other. The two component forces together have the same effect as the single force they replace.
Equilibrium
The situation in which the forces acting on an object are balanced, so the resultant force is zero. On a scale vector diagram the arrows representing the forces form a closed shape.
Nervous system
The system of receptors, neurones and the central nervous system that enables humans to react to their surroundings and to coordinate their behaviour.
Receptor
A cell or structure that detects a stimulus, for example the light receptors in the retina or the temperature receptors in the skin.
Neurone
A nerve cell that carries information as electrical impulses from receptors to the central nervous system, and from the central nervous system to effectors.
Central nervous system (CNS)
The brain and spinal cord. The CNS coordinates the response of effectors to the information it receives from receptors.
Effector
A structure that brings about the response. Effectors may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones.
Stimulus–response pathway
The sequence stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response, which describes how the body detects and responds to a change.
Reflex action
An automatic and rapid response to a stimulus that does not involve the conscious part of the brain.
Reflex arc
The pathway taken by an impulse in a reflex action: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone in the CNS → motor neurone → effector.
Synapse
The junction between two neurones. A chemical is released and diffuses across the gap, setting off a new electrical impulse in the next neurone.

physics-work-done-and-energy-transfer.d: Physics — Work done and energy transfer
terms: Work done

Work is done on an object when a force causes the object to move through a distance, that is when the force causes a displacement of the object. A force that produces no displacement does no work, however large the force is and however long it is applied for.
Distance moved along the line of action of the force

The distance s used in the work equation is the distance the object moves along the line of action of the force, not simply any distance it travels. Movement at right angles to the force contributes nothing to the work done by that force.
The work done equation

work done = force × distance (moved along the line of action of the force), written in symbols as W = F s, where work done, W, is in joules, J; force, F, is in newtons, N; and distance, s, is in metres.
Joule (J)
The unit of work done and of energy. One joule of work is done when a force of one newton causes a displacement of one metre.
Newton-metre (N m)

Force in newtons multiplied by distance in metres gives work in newton-metres. The newton-metre and the joule are the same size of unit: 1 joule = 1 newton-metre, so a value in N m converts to the identical number of J.
Energy transfer when work is done

Doing work is a way of transferring energy. When a force does work on an object, energy is transferred to that object, and the amount of energy transferred in joules is equal to the work done in joules.
Work done against friction
When an object moves against frictional forces, work is done against those forces. The energy transferred is not lost: it raises the temperature of the object rather than making it move faster.
Temperature rise from frictional work

Work done against the frictional forces acting on an object causes a rise in the temperature of the object, so surfaces such as brake blocks, rubbed hands and dragged crates become warmer as they move.
endocrine system
The system composed of glands which secrete chemicals called hormones directly into the bloodstream.
hormone
A chemical secreted by a gland directly into the bloodstream; the blood carries the hormone to a target organ where it produces an effect.
endocrine and nervous effects compared
Compared to the nervous system, the effects brought about by the endocrine system are slower but act for longer.
pituitary gland

A 'master gland' in the brain which secretes several hormones into the blood in response to body conditions; these hormones in turn act on other glands to stimulate other hormones to be released to bring about effects.
positions of the endocrine glands

On a diagram of the human body: the pituitary gland is in the brain; the thyroid is in the neck; the adrenal glands are on top of the kidneys; the pancreas lies behind the stomach; the ovaries are in the lower abdomen; the testes are below the abdomen in the scrotum.
pancreas
The gland that monitors and controls blood glucose concentration by producing hormones.
insulin
The hormone produced by the pancreas if the blood glucose concentration is too high; it causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells.
glycogen
The storage substance made in liver and muscle cells, where excess glucose is converted to glycogen for storage.
Type 1 diabetes
A disorder in which the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin, characterised by uncontrolled high blood glucose levels and normally treated with insulin injections.
Type 2 diabetes
A disorder in which the body cells no longer respond to insulin produced by the pancreas; a carbohydrate controlled diet and an exercise regime are common treatments, and obesity is a risk factor.
glucagon
The hormone produced by the pancreas if the blood glucose concentration is too low; it causes glycogen to be converted into glucose and released into the blood.
negative feedback

Control in which a level that has moved away from normal brings about a response that returns it to normal; it controls blood glucose through insulin and glucagon, the water level through ADH, and thyroxine levels.
secondary sex characteristics
The features that develop during puberty, caused by reproductive hormones.
oestrogen
The main female reproductive hormone, produced in the ovary; with progesterone it is involved in maintaining the uterus lining.
ovulation
The release of an egg from the ovary; from puberty eggs begin to mature and one is released approximately every 28 days.
testosterone
The main male reproductive hormone, produced by the testes; it stimulates sperm production.
follicle stimulating hormone (FSH)
A hormone involved in the menstrual cycle which causes maturation of an egg in the ovary.
luteinising hormone (LH)
A hormone involved in the menstrual cycle which stimulates the release of the egg.
progesterone
A hormone involved in the menstrual cycle which, with oestrogen, is involved in maintaining the uterus lining.
hormonal methods of contraception

Methods of controlling fertility that use hormones: oral contraceptives that contain hormones to inhibit FSH production so that no eggs mature; and injection, implant or skin patch of slow release progesterone to inhibit the maturation and release of eggs for a number of months or years. Some intrauterine devices also release a hormone.
non-hormonal methods of contraception

Methods of controlling fertility that do not use hormones: barrier methods such as condoms and diaphragms which prevent the sperm reaching an egg; intrauterine devices which prevent the implantation of an embryo; spermicidal agents which kill or disable sperm; abstaining from intercourse when an egg may be in the oviduct; and surgical methods of male and female sterilisation.
fertility drug
A drug containing FSH and LH given to a woman to treat infertility, after which she may become pregnant in the normal way.
In Vitro Fertilisation (IVF)

Fertility treatment in which a mother is given FSH and LH to stimulate the maturation of several eggs; the eggs are collected from the mother and fertilised by sperm from the father in the laboratory, the fertilised eggs develop into embryos, and at the stage when they are tiny balls of cells one or two embryos are inserted into the mother's uterus. It is very emotionally and physically stressful, the success rates are not high, and it can lead to multiple births which are a risk to both the babies and the mother.
adrenaline

A hormone produced by the adrenal glands in times of fear or stress; it increases the heart rate and boosts the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles, preparing the body for 'flight or fight'.
thyroxine
A hormone from the thyroid gland which stimulates the basal metabolic rate and plays an important role in growth and development; its level is controlled by negative feedback.
Deformation
A change in the shape of an object caused by forces acting on it. An object may be deformed by stretching it, by bending it or by compressing (squashing) it.
Stretching
Making an object longer by pulling its ends apart. Examples include a rubber band pulled between two hands and a spring hanging from a stand with a weight on the end.
Compressing
Making an object shorter by pushing its ends towards each other. Examples include the suspension spring of a parked car and a spring squashed between a hand and the bench.
Bending
Changing the shape of an object so that one side is stretched while the other side is compressed, for example a diving board pushed down at the free end while the fixed end is held.
Why more than one force is needed
To change the shape of a stationary object, more than one force must be applied. A single force would produce a resultant force, and the object would accelerate away instead of changing shape.
Elastic deformation
Deformation from which an object returns to its original shape and length once the deforming forces are removed.
Inelastic deformation
Deformation after which an object does not return to its original shape and length when the deforming forces are removed; it stays permanently changed.
Extension
The increase in length of an object compared with its original, unloaded length. Extension = stretched length - original length.
Directly proportional
Two quantities are directly proportional when a graph of one against the other is a straight line through the origin, so doubling one doubles the other.
Limit of proportionality
The point beyond which the extension of an object is no longer directly proportional to the force applied. Up to this point the force-extension graph is a straight line through the origin.
force = spring constant × extension
The relationship between the force applied to an elastic object and its extension, written as F = k e. It holds up to the limit of proportionality.
Force, F
The force applied to the spring, measured in newtons, N. For a spring hanging from a stand with masses on it, this force is the weight of the masses.
Spring constant, k
A measure of the stiffness of a spring: the force needed per metre of extension, measured in newtons per metre, N/m. A stiffer spring has a larger spring constant.
Extension, e
The extension used in F = k e, measured in metres, m. Lengths measured in centimetres or millimetres must be converted to metres before the equation is used.
Compression in F = k e
The same relationship applies when an elastic object is compressed. In that case e stands for the compression of the object rather than its extension.
Work done and elastic potential energy

A force that stretches or compresses a spring does work, and elastic potential energy is stored in the spring. Provided the spring is not inelastically deformed, the work done and the energy stored are equal.
Linear and non-linear relationships
A linear force-extension relationship gives a straight-line graph, so equal increases in force give equal increases in extension. A non-linear relationship gives a curve.
Spring constant from a graph
For a linear region, plotting force on the vertical axis against extension on the horizontal axis gives a straight line whose gradient is the spring constant, k.
elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × (extension)^2
The energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring, E_e = 1/2 k e^2, valid up to the limit of proportionality. Energy is in joules, J.
Energy transfer from a spring
When a stretched or compressed spring is released, the elastic potential energy stored in it is transferred to other stores, for example to the kinetic energy store of an object it pushes.
Required practical activity 6

An investigation of the relationship between force and extension for a spring: hang the spring from a stand, add known weights one at a time, and measure the length after each weight so that the extension can be found.
AT 1 and AT 2 in this practical
AT 1 is the use of apparatus to make length measurements; AT 2 is the safe use of apparatus to measure force. Both are used when a ruler and known weights are used on a loaded spring.
Working scientifically and maths skills here
The practical develops skills such as tabulating results, plotting force against extension, drawing a line of best fit, finding a gradient and identifying anomalous results.

physics-forces-and-motion-describing-mot.d: Physics — Forces and motion: Describing motion along a line
terms: Distance
Distance is how far an object moves along the path it actually travels. It does not involve direction, so it is a scalar quantity: a magnitude and a unit fully describe it, for example 450 m.
Displacement

Displacement is the distance an object moves measured in a straight line from the start point to the finish point, together with the direction of that straight line. It is quoted as a magnitude and a direction, for example 450 m due east.
Scalar quantity
A scalar quantity has magnitude only. Distance and speed are scalars: stating the number and the unit says everything there is to say about them.
Vector quantity
A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction. Displacement and velocity are vectors: two vectors of the same size pointing different ways are different quantities.
Speed
Speed is how fast an object is moving. It does not involve direction, so speed is a scalar quantity, measured in metres per second, m/s.
Typical speeds of a person
The specification gives typical values that may be taken as: walking about 1.5 m/s, running about 3 m/s and cycling about 6 m/s. These are estimates to be recalled and used, not exact figures.
Typical speeds of transport systems

Students should also be able to recall typical speeds for different types of transportation system, for example a car on a motorway at roughly 30 m/s, a train at roughly 50 m/s and an aeroplane at roughly 250 m/s.
Factors affecting a person's speed
The speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle depends on many factors including age, terrain, fitness and the distance travelled.
Varying speed

The speed of a moving object is rarely constant: when people walk, run or travel in a car their speed changes constantly. It is not only moving objects that have varying speed, because the speed of sound and the speed of the wind also vary.
Speed of sound in air
A typical value for the speed of sound in air is 330 m/s. The actual value varies, for example with the temperature of the air.
Measuring speed
Speed is found by measuring a distance, for example with a ruler, tape measure or trundle wheel, measuring the time taken with a stopwatch or light gates, and then dividing the distance by the time.
Distance travelled at constant speed
For an object moving at constant speed the distance travelled in a specific time can be calculated using distance travelled = speed × time, written in symbols as [s = v t].
Quantities and units in [s = v t]
In s = v t the distance s is in metres, m; the speed v is in metres per second, m/s; and the time t is in seconds, s.
Average speed
For non-uniform motion the average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken, including any time spent stationary.
Velocity
The velocity of an object is its speed in a given direction, so velocity is a vector quantity. Two objects with equal speeds have different velocities if they move in different directions.
Vector-scalar distinction in motion
Distance and speed are scalars; displacement and velocity are the matching vector quantities. Each pair has the same unit, and the vector member of the pair also carries a direction.
Motion in a circle (HT only)

An object moving in a circle at a steady rate has constant speed but changing velocity, because its direction of motion changes continuously. Examples include a car on a roundabout and a satellite in a circular orbit.
Distance-time graph
If an object moves along a straight line, the distance travelled can be represented by a distance-time graph, with time on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical axis.
Gradient of a distance-time graph

The speed of an object can be calculated from the gradient of its distance-time graph: gradient is the change in distance divided by the change in time. A horizontal line has zero gradient, so the object is stationary.
Tangent to a distance-time graph (HT only)
If an object is accelerating, its speed at any particular time can be determined by drawing a tangent to the curve at that time and measuring the gradient of that tangent.
Drawing and interpreting distance-time graphs
Students should be able to draw distance-time graphs from measurements, and extract and interpret lines and slopes, translating information between graphical and numerical form.
Average acceleration
The average acceleration of an object can be calculated using acceleration = (change in velocity)/(time taken), written in symbols as [a = (∆v)/(t)].
Quantities and units in [a = (∆v)/(t)]
Acceleration, a, is in metres per second squared, m/s^2; change in velocity, ∆ v, is in metres per second, m/s; and time, t, is in seconds, s.
Deceleration
An object that slows down is decelerating. Its acceleration has the opposite sign to its velocity, so for an object moving forwards the acceleration is negative.
Everyday accelerations
Students should be able to estimate the magnitude of everyday accelerations, for example a family car pulling away at roughly 2 m/s^2 and an object falling freely at about 9.8 m/s^2.
Gradient of a velocity-time graph

The acceleration of an object can be calculated from the gradient of a velocity-time graph. Students should be able to draw velocity-time graphs from measurements and interpret lines and slopes to determine acceleration.
Area under a velocity-time graph (HT only)
