The distance travelled by an object, or the displacement of an object, can be calculated from the area under a velocity-time graph, and students should be able to interpret enclosed areas to determine it.
Counting squares (HT only)
Where the area under a velocity-time graph is not a simple triangle or rectangle, it can be measured, when appropriate, by counting squares and multiplying by the quantity one square represents.
Uniform acceleration equation
The following equation applies to uniform acceleration: (final velocity)^2 - (initial velocity)^2 = 2 × acceleration × distance, written in symbols as [v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s].
Quantities and units in [v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s]
Final velocity v and initial velocity u are in metres per second, m/s; acceleration a is in metres per second squared, m/s^2; and distance s is in metres, m.
Acceleration of free fall
Near the Earth's surface any object falling freely under gravity has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s^2, whatever its mass.
Terminal velocity

An object falling through a fluid initially accelerates due to the force of gravity. As it speeds up the drag force grows until eventually the resultant force is zero and the object moves at its terminal velocity. Physics only: students should be able to draw and interpret velocity-time graphs for objects that reach terminal velocity and interpret the changing motion in terms of the forces acting.

physics-forces-and-motion-forces-acceler.d: Physics — Forces and motion: Forces, accelerations and Newton's Laws of motion
terms: Newton's First Law

If the resultant force acting on an object is zero, the object's motion does not change: a stationary object remains stationary and a moving object continues to move at the same speed and in the same direction, so at the same velocity. The law is about the resultant of the forces being zero, not about there being no forces at all.
Zero resultant force

The single force that would have the same effect as all the forces acting on an object together. When the forces balance, that resultant is zero: a stationary object then remains stationary, even though individual forces such as weight and a surface's upward push are still acting on it.
Uniform velocity

Motion at the same speed in the same direction. If the resultant force on a moving object is zero, the object continues to move at the same speed and in the same direction, so it continues to move at the same velocity. No forward force is needed to maintain that motion.
Steady speed of a vehicle

When a vehicle travels at a steady speed the resistive forces balance the driving force. The driving force from the engine and the resistive forces of friction and air resistance are equal in size and opposite in direction, so the resultant force is zero and the velocity does not change.
Change of velocity

The velocity (speed and/or direction) of an object will only change if a resultant force is acting on the object. A car rounding a bend at a constant speed has a changing direction, so its velocity is changing and a resultant force must be acting, even though the speedometer reading is fixed.
Inertia

The tendency of objects to continue in their state of rest or of uniform motion is called inertia. It is a tendency, not a force: passengers thrown forwards when a bus brakes are not pushed forwards, they simply keep moving at the velocity they already had while the bus slows beneath them.
Newton's Second Law

The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force acting on the object, and inversely proportional to the mass of the object. Doubling the resultant force on a fixed mass doubles the acceleration; doubling the mass under a fixed resultant force halves the acceleration.
resultant force = mass x acceleration

Newton's Second Law written as an equation: resultant force = mass x acceleration, F = m a. The F in the equation is the resultant of all the forces on the object, not any single force acting on it, and the equation can be rearranged to find the mass or the acceleration.
Units in F = m a

In the equation F = m a the force, F, is in newtons, N; the mass, m, is in kilograms, kg; and the acceleration, a, is in metres per second squared, m/s^2. A mass given in grams must be converted to kilograms before it is substituted into the equation.
Inertial mass

Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object. A large inertial mass needs a large resultant force to produce a given change of velocity, which is why a loaded lorry is far harder to speed up or slow down than a bicycle.
Inertial mass as a ratio

Inertial mass is defined as the ratio of force over acceleration. Dividing the resultant force acting on an object by the acceleration that force produces gives the object's inertial mass in kilograms, which is the same rearrangement as m = F / a taken from F = m a.
Estimating road transport quantities

Typical everyday values let speeds, accelerations and forces be estimated for road transport: a car reaching about 27 m/s in about 9 s accelerates at roughly 3 m/s^2, and with a mass of about 1000 kg that needs a resultant force of roughly 3000 N. Large accelerations demand correspondingly large forces.
The approximation symbol

The symbol ~ placed before a value indicates an approximate value or an approximate answer. Writing 'resultant force ~ 3000 N' says the figure is an estimate of the right order, obtained from rounded data, and not a precisely measured or exactly calculated result.
Required practical activity 7: force and acceleration

An investigation of the effect of varying the force on the acceleration of an object of constant mass. A trolley is pulled by hanging masses on a string over a pulley and the acceleration is found from light gate timings. The total mass being accelerated must be kept constant, so masses are moved from the trolley to the hanger to change the force.
Required practical activity 7: mass and acceleration

The second part of the same practical investigates the effect of varying the mass of an object on the acceleration produced by a constant force. With the pulling force fixed, extra masses are added to the trolley and the acceleration is measured each time; the acceleration falls as the mass rises, because acceleration is inversely proportional to mass.
Newton's Third Law

Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite. If a swimmer pushes back on the water with 200 N, the water pushes the swimmer forwards with 200 N. The two forces are always the same size, whatever the sizes of the two objects.
Third law pair in equilibrium

In an equilibrium situation such as a book resting on a table, the third law pair is the book's downward push on the table and the table's upward push on the book. These act on different objects, so they never cancel; the book's weight and the table's upward push act on the same object and are balanced forces, not a third law pair.

physics-forces-and-motion-forces-and-bra.d: Physics — Forces and motion: Forces and braking
terms: Stopping distance
The total distance a vehicle travels from the moment the driver sees a hazard to the moment the vehicle comes to rest: stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance.
Thinking distance

The distance the vehicle travels during the driver's reaction time, before the brakes are applied. The vehicle is still moving at its full speed throughout, so thinking distance = speed x reaction time.
Braking distance
The distance the vehicle travels under the braking force, from the moment the brakes are applied to the moment the vehicle comes to rest.
Effect of speed on stopping distance

For a given braking force, the greater the speed of the vehicle the greater the stopping distance. Thinking distance grows in proportion to speed; braking distance grows faster still, because the same force must remove kinetic energy that depends on speed squared.
Emergency stop estimate

A rough stopping distance for a vehicle at a typical road speed, found by adding an estimated thinking distance (speed x about 0.7 s) to an estimated braking distance. For a car, about 23 m at 13 m/s (30 mph) and about 96 m at 31 m/s (70 mph).
Speed-stopping distance graph

A graph of stopping distance against speed for a vehicle. The thinking distance contribution is a straight line through the origin; the braking distance contribution curves upwards, so the total line gets steeper as speed increases. A heavier vehicle sits above a lighter one at every speed.
Reaction time
The time between a driver seeing a hazard and beginning to act on it. Reaction times vary from person to person, with typical values ranging from 0.2 s to 0.9 s.
Factors affecting reaction time
Tiredness, drugs and alcohol lengthen a driver's reaction time. Distractions, such as using a phone or a loud conversation, may also affect the driver's ability to react.
Ruler drop test

A simple method of measuring human reaction time: one student releases a ruler between another's open finger and thumb without warning, and the distance the ruler falls before it is caught is converted into a time. A shorter drop means a shorter reaction time.
Computer reaction timer

A method in which a computer displays a signal at a random moment and records how long the user takes to click. It gives a time directly in seconds and removes the human error involved in judging and converting a ruler drop.
Repeats, means and anomalies

Reaction time varies from trial to trial, so several trials are made and a mean is taken, with any anomalous result identified and excluded from the mean. This makes a comparison between two students, or before and after a change, more reliable.
Adverse road and weather conditions
Wet or icy road conditions reduce the grip between the tyres and the road, so the braking force that can be applied without skidding is smaller and the braking distance is longer.
Poor condition of the vehicle
For this specification, poor condition of the vehicle means worn or faulty brakes, or worn or badly inflated tyres. Either one increases the braking distance.
Implications for road safety

Because stopping distance grows sharply with speed, and grows further in poor conditions, safe driving means lowering speed and leaving a larger gap when the road is wet or icy, and keeping brakes and tyres in good order.
Work done by the braking friction force
When a force is applied to the brakes, work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel reduces the kinetic energy of the vehicle and the temperature of the brakes increases.
Braking force for a given distance
The greater the speed of a vehicle the greater the braking force needed to stop the vehicle in a certain distance, because more kinetic energy has to be removed over the same distance.
Deceleration
The rate at which a vehicle's velocity decreases. The greater the braking force the greater the deceleration of the vehicle.
Dangers of large decelerations
Large decelerations require very large braking forces. These may lead to the brakes overheating and/or loss of control of the vehicle, for example if the wheels lock and the vehicle skids.
Estimating braking forces

For a road vehicle the braking force can be estimated from the mass and the deceleration using F = m a, after finding the deceleration from the change in velocity and the time taken. Emergency braking of a family car gives decelerations of a few m/s2 up to about 10 m/s2 and forces of the order of 10 000 N.
Closed system

A system in which no mass enters or leaves and no external resultant force acts. Conservation of momentum is stated by the specification for a closed system, and it is that condition which makes the total momentum before and after an event equal.
Conservation of momentum

The name given to the statement that, in a closed system, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after the event. It applies to the total for the whole system, not to each object separately.
Event (collision)

Anything that changes how the objects in a system are moving: a collision, objects sticking together, or an explosion pushing objects apart. Momentum is used as a model to describe and explain what happens in such an event.
Explosion and recoil

An event in which objects initially at rest push each other apart. The total momentum before is zero, so the total momentum after must also be zero: the two objects move in opposite directions with momenta of equal size.
Meiosis

The type of cell division that leads to non-identical cells being formed. It takes place in the reproductive organs to form gametes, and all the gametes produced are genetically different from each other.
Mitosis

The type of cell division that leads to identical cells being formed. It is the only division involved in asexual reproduction, and it is the division by which the new cell formed at fertilisation increases the number of cells.
Sexual reproduction
Reproduction involving the joining (fusion) of male and female gametes. Because there is mixing of genetic information from two parents, it leads to variety in the offspring.
Gamete

A sex cell that joins with another gamete at fertilisation. In animals the gametes are sperm and egg cells; in flowering plants they are pollen and egg cells. A gamete contains a single set of chromosomes.
Asexual reproduction
Reproduction involving only one parent and no fusion of gametes. There is no mixing of genetic information, only mitosis is involved, and the offspring are genetically identical to the parent.
Clone
An offspring that is genetically identical to its parent. Clones are produced by asexual reproduction because only mitosis is involved and there is no mixing of genetic information.
Formation of gametes

Cells in the reproductive organs divide by meiosis to form gametes. Copies of the genetic information are made, then the cell divides twice to form four gametes, each with a single set of chromosomes and all genetically different from each other.
Fertilisation
The joining of two gametes, which restores the normal number of chromosomes. Meiosis halves the chromosome number in the gametes, so fertilisation of two gametes brings the full number back.
Differentiation in the embryo
After fertilisation the new cell divides by mitosis so the number of cells increases. As the embryo develops these cells differentiate, becoming specialised for different jobs.
DNA
The chemical of which the genetic material in the nucleus of a cell is composed. DNA is a polymer made up of two strands forming a double helix, and it is contained in structures called chromosomes.
Chromosome
A structure in the nucleus that contains the DNA. Genes are carried as small sections of DNA along a chromosome.
Gene
A small section of DNA on a chromosome. Each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, to make a specific protein.
Genome
The entire genetic material of an organism. The whole human genome has now been studied and this will have great importance for medicine in the future.
Importance of understanding the human genome

Understanding the human genome matters for three reasons: the search for genes linked to different types of disease, the understanding and treatment of inherited disorders, and its use in tracing human migration patterns from the past.
Allele
One of the different forms a gene may have. Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene, such as fur colour in mice and red-green colour blindness in humans.
Dominant allele
An allele that is always expressed, even if only one copy is present.
Recessive allele
An allele that is only expressed if two copies are present, and therefore no dominant allele is present.
Homozygous
Describes an organism in which the two alleles present for a trait are the same.
Heterozygous
Describes an organism in which the two alleles present for a trait are different.
Genotype
The alleles present in an organism. The genotype operates at a molecular level to develop characteristics.
Phenotype
The characteristics that the genotype develops and that are expressed in the organism.
Multiple gene inheritance
Most characteristics are a result of multiple genes interacting, rather than a single gene, so most phenotype features are not the result of single gene inheritance.
Punnett square

A diagram used to set out a genetic cross by combining the alleles carried by the gametes of each parent. The outcome can be expressed using direct proportion or simple ratios, and gives the probability of each genotype rather than a guaranteed result.
Inherited disorders

Disorders caused by the inheritance of certain alleles. Polydactyly, having extra fingers or toes, is caused by a dominant allele. Cystic fibrosis, a disorder of cell membranes, is caused by a recessive allele.
Embryo screening

Screening embryos for the alleles that cause inherited disorders. It raises economic, social and ethical issues about which students should make informed judgements when given appropriate information.
Sex chromosomes

Ordinary human body cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes. 22 pairs control characteristics only, but one of the pairs carries the genes that determine sex: in females the sex chromosomes are the same (XX) and in males they are different (XY).
Rate of reaction
How quickly a reaction proceeds. It can be found by measuring the quantity of a reactant used or the quantity of product formed over time.
Mean rate of reaction
The average rate over a period of time: mean rate of reaction = (quantity of reactant used) / (time taken), or (quantity of product formed) / (time taken).
Quantity of reactant used
How much of a starting substance has been consumed in a given time, measured as a mass in grams or as a volume in cm³ (moles at Higher Tier).
Quantity of product formed
How much of a new substance has been made in a given time, measured as a mass in grams or as a volume in cm³ (moles at Higher Tier).
Units of rate of reaction
The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s or cm³ /s, because a quantity is divided by a time.
Rate in mol/s (Higher Tier)
At Higher Tier the quantity of reactants may be given in moles, and the rate of reaction is then given in mol/s.
Quantity-time graph (volume-time or mass-time)
A graph of the quantity of product formed, or of reactant used up, plotted against time. Its steepness at any point shows how fast the reaction is going.
Tangent
A straight line drawn so that it just touches a curve at one point. Its slope is used as a measure of the rate of reaction at that moment.
Gradient of a tangent (Higher Tier)
The change in the y quantity divided by the change in time along the tangent, calculated as a measure of rate of reaction at a specific time.
Factors affecting rate
The concentrations of reactants in solution, the pressure of reacting gases, the surface area of solid reactants, the temperature and the presence of catalysts.
Concentration
The amount of a dissolved substance in a given volume of solution. A more concentrated solution has more reactant particles in the same volume.
Pressure of reacting gases
How tightly gas particles are packed. Raising the pressure of reacting gases puts more particles into the same volume.
Surface area of solid reactants
The area of solid exposed to the other reactant. Breaking a solid into smaller pieces exposes more of it.
Turbidity
The cloudiness of a mixture. A reaction that makes an insoluble solid grows cloudy, and the time for a mark to disappear can be timed.
Hypothesis
A testable prediction about how one variable will affect another, which the investigation is then designed to test.
Collision theory
Chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy.
Frequency of collisions
How many collisions happen each second. Increasing it increases the rate of reaction.
Activation energy
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react.
Surface area to volume ratio
The surface area of a solid divided by its volume. Smaller pieces of the same mass have a larger surface area to volume ratio.
Proportionality in rate
A simple idea used with collision theory: doubling the number of particles in a given volume roughly doubles the collision frequency, and so roughly doubles the rate.
Catalyst
A substance that changes the rate of a chemical reaction but is not used up during the reaction. Different reactions need different catalysts.
Enzyme
A biological catalyst. Enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems.
Reaction pathway
The route a reaction takes from reactants to products. A catalyst provides a different pathway that has a lower activation energy.
Reaction profile
An energy diagram for a reaction. For a catalysed reaction it is drawn with a lower hump, while the reactants and products stay at the same energies.

physics-waves-in-air-fluids-and-solids-t.d: Physics — Waves in air, fluids and solids: Transverse and longitudinal waves
terms: Transverse wave
A wave in which the oscillations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer. Ripples on a water surface are an example of a transverse wave.
Longitudinal wave
A wave in which the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer. Longitudinal waves show areas of compression and rarefaction, and sound travelling through air is longitudinal.
Oscillation

The repeated back-and-forth or up-and-down movement of a particle of the medium about a fixed position as a wave passes. The direction of this oscillation compared with the direction the wave travels is what separates the two types of wave.
Compression
A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles of the medium are pushed closer together than normal, so the medium there is at a higher pressure.
Rarefaction

A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles of the medium are spread further apart than normal, so the medium there is at a lower pressure. The particles are still present; a rarefaction is not an empty space.
Ripple
A wave on a water surface. Each part of the surface moves up and down while the ripple travels outwards, which is what makes it a transverse wave.
Sound wave in air
A longitudinal wave in which the air is repeatedly pushed together and pulled apart, producing compressions and rarefactions that travel away from the source.
Energy transfer without matter transfer
A wave moves energy from place to place while the water or air it passes through only oscillates about a fixed position and is not carried along with the wave.

physics-waves-in-air-fluids-and-solids-p.d: Physics — Waves in air, fluids and solids: Properties of waves
terms: Describing wave motion

Any wave, transverse or longitudinal, is described using four quantities: amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period. Amplitude describes the size of the oscillation; wavelength describes how long one complete wave is; frequency and period describe its timing and are two ways of stating the same information, since T = 1/f. Wave speed is a further quantity, but it is calculated from frequency and wavelength rather than being one of the four descriptive quantities.
Amplitude

The amplitude of a wave is the maximum displacement of a point on a wave away from its undisturbed position. It is measured from the undisturbed line up to a crest, or from the undisturbed line down to a trough — never from a trough all the way up to a crest, which is twice the amplitude. Amplitude is a distance and is read on the displacement axis of a wave diagram.
Undisturbed position

The undisturbed position is where a point in the medium would sit if no wave were passing — its rest position. On a wave diagram it is the centre line about which the wave oscillates, and it is the line from which amplitude is measured. Displacement is measured from this line, so a point at the undisturbed position has zero displacement even though the wave is still passing.
Wavelength

The wavelength of a wave is the distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave. Crest to the next crest, trough to the next trough, or any point to the matching point one wave later all give the same distance. Wavelength is given the symbol λ and measured in metres, m. A crest to the neighbouring trough is only half a wavelength.
Frequency

The frequency of a wave is the number of waves passing a point each second. It is a counting rate — not a speed, and not a count of how many waves happen to be drawn on a diagram. Frequency is given the symbol f and measured in hertz, Hz, where 1 Hz means one complete wave passing each second.
Period

The period of a wave is the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point, and it is the reciprocal of the frequency: period = (1)/(frequency). A high frequency therefore means a short period. A wave of frequency 8 Hz has a period of 1/8 = 0.125 s, because eight waves share each second.
T = 1/f and its rearrangement

The specification states the relationship as period = (1)/(frequency), in symbols [T = 1/f]. Because the two quantities are reciprocals, the relationship rearranges to f = 1/T, so either can be found from the other. A period of 0.004 s gives f = 1/0.004 = 250 Hz. Period and frequency are never equal in value unless both are 1.
Unit of period

The specification gives period, T, in seconds, s. Period is a time, so its unit is the second — the same unit as any other time interval. Periods of waves are often small fractions of a second, so answers such as 0.004 s are normal and should not be rounded to zero or converted into hertz.
Hertz

The specification gives frequency, f, in hertz, Hz. One hertz is one complete wave passing a point each second. Larger frequencies are often quoted in kilohertz, kHz, or megahertz, MHz: 1 kHz = 1000 Hz and 1 MHz = 1 000 000 Hz, so a frequency in kHz is multiplied by 1000 to convert it into hertz before it is used in the wave equation.
Wave speed

The wave speed is the speed at which the energy is transferred (or the wave moves) through the medium. It is not the speed of the particles of the medium, which only oscillate about their undisturbed positions and are not carried along with the wave. Wave speed is given the symbol v and measured in metres per second, m/s.
All waves obey the wave equation

All waves obey the wave equation: it holds for transverse and longitudinal waves alike, and for waves in air, in fluids and in solids. Sound, ripples on water, waves on a string and electromagnetic waves are all covered by the same relationship, so a single equation links speed, frequency and wavelength for every wave met in this course.
The wave equation

The wave equation is wave speed = frequency × wavelength, in symbols [v = f λ]. It rearranges to f = v/λ and to λ = v/f. Because the speed is a product of the other two, a wave that keeps the same speed has a wavelength that falls as its frequency rises. Substituting f in Hz and λ in m always gives v in m/s.
Units in the wave equation

The specification gives wave speed, v, in metres per second, m/s; frequency, f, in hertz, Hz; and wavelength, λ, in metres, m. The equation only produces a speed in m/s if the wavelength is entered in metres and the frequency in hertz, so a wavelength quoted in centimetres or millimetres must be converted first, and a frequency in kilohertz must be multiplied by 1000.
Reading amplitude and wavelength from a diagram

On a displacement–distance graph, amplitude is read vertically on the displacement axis, from the undisturbed centre line to a crest or trough, while wavelength is read horizontally on the distance axis, from one point to the equivalent point on the next wave. The two quantities are therefore measured on different axes, and confusing the axes is the commonest error when identifying them from a given diagram.
Measuring the speed of sound in air

A workable method is to stand a measured distance from a large reflecting wall, clap, and time the echo returning; the sound has travelled twice the distance to the wall, so wave speed = (2 × distance) ÷ time. Distances of many tens of metres, and timings taken over several claps, are used so that human reaction time is small compared with the time being measured. An alternative method uses two microphones a measured distance apart connected to an electronic timer.
Measuring the speed of ripples on a water surface

A ripple tank with a vibrating dipper produces ripples whose pattern is projected onto a screen below. The frequency is read from the signal generator driving the dipper, and the wavelength is measured with a ruler laid against the projected pattern, ideally across ten wavelengths which are then divided by ten. The wave speed is then found from v = f λ. A stroboscope or a video frame freezes the moving pattern so that it can be measured.
Sound passing from one medium to another

When a sound wave crosses from one medium into another, its frequency is fixed by the vibrating source and does not change. The wave speed does change, because it depends on the medium — sound travels faster in water, and faster still in solids, than in air. Since v = f λ and f is fixed, the wavelength must change in the same proportion as the speed: a faster medium gives a longer wavelength.
Required practical activity 8

In this practical, observations are made to identify the suitability of apparatus for measuring the frequency, wavelength and speed of waves in a ripple tank and of waves in a solid, and appropriate measurements are taken. Typical judgements include using a ruler on the projected pattern rather than a stopwatch on a single ripple, reading the frequency from the signal generator, and measuring across ten wavelengths on a stretched string before dividing by ten.
Phenotype
The characteristics of an organism. The phenotype develops as a result of the genome of the organism and its interaction with the environment.
Variation

Differences in the characteristics of individuals in a population. Variation may be due to the genes they have inherited (genetic causes), the conditions in which they have developed (environmental causes), or a combination of genes and the environment.
Mutation

A change in the DNA of an organism. All variants arise from mutations, and mutations occur continuously. Very rarely a mutation will lead to a new phenotype, and if that new phenotype is suited to an environmental change it can lead to a relatively rapid change in the species.
Effect of mutations on the phenotype

There is usually extensive genetic variation within a population of a species. Of the variants that arise from mutations, most have no effect on the phenotype, some influence phenotype and very few determine phenotype.
Evolution
A change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time through a process of natural selection, which may result in the formation of a new species.
Natural selection

The process by which variants that give rise to phenotypes best suited to their environment are the most likely to survive and to breed successfully, so that the genes for these characteristics are passed on to the next generation.
Theory of evolution by natural selection
The theory that all species of living things have evolved from simple life forms that first developed more than three billion years ago.
Formation of a new species
Two populations of one species have formed two new species when they become so different in phenotype that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
Selective breeding (artificial selection)

The process by which humans breed plants and animals for particular genetic characteristics. Parents with the desired characteristic are chosen from a mixed population and bred together; from the offspring, those with the desired characteristic are bred together, and this continues over many generations until all the offspring show the desired characteristic. Humans have done this for thousands of years, since they first bred food crops from wild plants and domesticated animals.
Desired characteristic

The characteristic that humans select for in selective breeding, chosen for usefulness or appearance. Examples are disease resistance in food crops, animals which produce more meat or milk, domestic dogs with a gentle nature, and large or unusual flowers.
Inbreeding
Breeding from closely related individuals, which selective breeding can lead to. Some breeds produced in this way are particularly prone to disease or inherited defects.
Genetic engineering

A process which involves modifying the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism to give a desired characteristic. Genes from the chromosomes of humans and other organisms can be 'cut out' and transferred to cells of other organisms.
Genetically modified (GM) crops

Crops that have had their genes modified by genetic engineering. GM crops include ones that are resistant to insect attack or to herbicides, and GM crops generally show increased yields. Plant crops have also been genetically engineered to be resistant to diseases or to produce bigger better fruits. Concerns about GM crops include the effect on populations of wild flowers and insects, and some people feel that the effects of eating GM crops on human health have not been fully explored.
Genetically engineered bacteria
Bacterial cells that have been genetically engineered to produce useful substances, such as human insulin to treat diabetes.
Genetic modification and inherited disorders
Modern medical research is exploring the possibility of genetic modification to overcome some inherited disorders.
Vector

In genetic engineering, the structure that carries the required gene into cells, usually a bacterial plasmid or a virus. Enzymes are used to isolate the required gene, the gene is inserted into the vector, and the vector is used to insert the gene into the required cells. Genes are transferred to the cells of animals, plants or microorganisms at an early stage in their development so that they develop with the desired characteristics.

chemistry-reversible-reactions-and-dynam.d: Chemistry — Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium
terms: Reversible reaction

A reaction in which the products of the reaction can react to produce the original reactants. Once some product has formed it is able to change back into the starting substances, so the change is not a one-way dead end.
The ⇌ symbol

The double arrow used to represent a reversible reaction, written A + B ⇌ C + D. It shows that the change can run in the forward direction and in the reverse direction; it does not say how much of each substance is present.
Thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride
The specification's example of a reversible reaction: ammonium chloride ⇌ ammonia + hydrogen chloride. Heating the white solid gives the two gases, and cooling the gases forms the white solid again.
Closed system
Apparatus which prevents the escape of reactants and products, so that everything made by the forward reaction stays in the mixture and is available for the reverse reaction.
Equilibrium

The state reached in a closed system when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate. Both reactions are still happening, so the amounts of the substances stay constant rather than becoming equal.
Position of equilibrium

A description of the relative amounts of reactants and products present at equilibrium. Moving towards the products is called shifting to the right; moving towards the reactants is shifting to the left.
Le Chatelier's Principle

The idea that if a system is at equilibrium and a change is made to any of the conditions, the system responds to counteract the change. It is used to predict the effect of changes on systems at equilibrium.
Counteracting a change
The system shifts in the direction that opposes what was done to it, reducing the effect of the change without cancelling it completely, so the new equilibrium is different from the original one.
Effect of a concentration change

If the concentration of a reactant is increased, more products are formed until equilibrium is reached again; if the concentration of a product is decreased, more reactants react until equilibrium is reached again.
Effect of a temperature change

Raising the temperature increases the relative amount of products for an endothermic reaction and decreases it for an exothermic reaction. Lowering the temperature has the opposite effect in each case.
Effect of a pressure change

For gaseous reactions, an increase in pressure shifts the equilibrium position towards the side with the smaller number of molecules, and a decrease in pressure shifts it towards the side with the larger number.
Counting molecules from the symbol equation
The numbers of gas molecules on each side of an equilibrium are read from the balancing numbers in the symbol equation, so 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3 has three molecules on the left and two on the right.
Electromagnetic wave
A transverse wave that transfers energy from the source of the wave to an absorber. Electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum, so no substance is needed to carry them.
Transverse wave
A wave in which the oscillations are at right angles to the direction in which the wave transfers energy. All electromagnetic waves are transverse.
Energy transfer by a wave
A wave moves energy from one place to another without moving matter from one place to another. The particles or fields oscillate; they are not carried along.
Source and absorber
The source is the object that emits the wave; the absorber is the object that takes in its energy. A lamp is a source of light; a black surface it shines on is an absorber.
Continuous spectrum

The electromagnetic spectrum has no gaps: wavelength changes smoothly from very long to very short, and the seven named groups are labelled regions of one continuous range, not seven separate wave types.
Wavelength
The distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave. Radio waves have the longest wavelength in the spectrum and gamma rays the shortest.
Frequency
The number of waves passing a point each second. Across the spectrum frequency rises as wavelength falls, so gamma rays have the highest frequency and radio waves the lowest.
Visible light
The only group of electromagnetic waves the human eye can detect. Within it, red has the longest wavelength and violet the shortest, so the group runs red to violet.
Vacuum
A space containing no matter. All types of electromagnetic wave travel at the same velocity through a vacuum (space) or air, which is why sunlight reaches the Earth across empty space.
Absorption of an electromagnetic wave

When a wave meets a substance and its energy is transferred into that substance instead of continuing through it. The wave does not emerge on the far side and the internal energy of the substance increases.
Transmission of an electromagnetic wave

When a wave passes through a substance and emerges on the other side. A substance that transmits a wave lets it carry on, although the velocity of the wave inside the substance may differ from its velocity outside.
Reflection of an electromagnetic wave

When a wave meets a boundary and travels back into the substance it came from rather than entering the new substance. Reflection is a third possibility alongside absorption and transmission, and in general all three happen at once in different proportions.
Variation with wavelength

Whether a particular substance absorbs, transmits, refracts or reflects an electromagnetic wave is not a single fixed property of that substance: it varies with the wavelength of the wave. Glass transmits visible light but absorbs much of the ultraviolet, and brick transmits radio waves but not visible light.
Refraction

The change of direction of a wave as it crosses the boundary between two substances at an angle to the normal. It is one of the effects a substance can have on a wave, alongside absorbing, transmitting and reflecting it.
Difference in velocity as the cause of refraction

Some effects, for example refraction, are due to the difference in velocity of the waves in different substances. If a wave had the same velocity in both substances it would cross the boundary without changing direction, however steep the angle.
What changes and what does not at a boundary

The frequency of a wave is set by its source and does not change when the wave enters a new substance. The velocity does change, so the wavelength must change with it: a wave that slows down has a shorter wavelength in the new substance.
Normal

A construction line drawn at right angles to the boundary at the exact point where the ray meets it, usually shown dashed. Every angle in a refraction ray diagram is measured from the normal, never from the boundary itself.
Angle of incidence and angle of refraction
The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal. The angle of refraction is the angle between the refracted ray and the normal, measured on the far side of the boundary.
Constructing a ray diagram for refraction

Draw the boundary, add the dashed normal where the ray strikes it, draw the incident ray with an arrow towards the boundary, then draw the refracted ray continuing from that same point with an arrow away from it. A ray entering a substance in which it travels more slowly bends towards the normal; one entering a substance in which it travels faster bends away from the normal; a ray along the normal is not deviated.
Wave front

A line joining points of a wave that are all in phase with one another, for example all the crests. Wave fronts are drawn at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels, and the spacing between them is the wavelength.
Explaining refraction with a wave front diagram

When wave fronts meet a boundary at an angle, one end of each front crosses into the new medium before the other end does. If the wave travels more slowly in the new medium that end is held back while the rest of the front is still moving at the old speed, so the front pivots and the whole wave changes direction. The fronts also become closer together, because the wavelength falls with the speed.
Infrared radiation

Electromagnetic radiation emitted by all objects because of their temperature, and the radiation investigated in Required practical activity 10. A hotter object emits infrared at a greater rate than a cooler one.
How the nature of a surface affects infrared

A matt black surface is the best absorber of infrared radiation and also the best emitter of it. A shiny, silvered or pale surface is a poor absorber and a poor emitter, and reflects most of the infrared that reaches it. A good absorber is always a good emitter.
Leslie cube

A hollow metal cube whose four vertical faces are given different surfaces, for example matt black, matt white, shiny silver and dull grey. Filling it with hot water puts every face at the same temperature, so any difference in the infrared detected must be caused by the nature of the surface.
Control variables in Required practical activity 10

The nature of the surface is the independent variable, so everything else must be kept the same: the temperature of the water, the distance from the surface to the detector, the orientation of the detector and the time allowed before each reading is taken. Changing any of these alongside the surface makes the comparison invalid.
Oscillation in an electrical circuit

A repeated back-and-forth change in the current in a circuit, so that charge flows first one way and then the other, over and over again. The number of complete back-and-forth cycles each second is the frequency of the oscillation.
Production of radio waves

(HT only) Radio waves can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits. A circuit made to oscillate at a chosen frequency drives charge back and forth in a transmitting aerial, and radio waves of that frequency are sent out.
Induced alternating current

(HT only) When radio waves are absorbed they may create an alternating current in a circuit — a current that repeatedly reverses direction rather than flowing steadily one way. In this sense radio waves can themselves induce oscillations in an electrical circuit.
Frequency match on absorption

(HT only) The alternating current created when a radio wave is absorbed has the same frequency as the radio wave itself. A 200 MHz wave absorbed by a receiving aerial sets up an alternating current of 200 MHz in the circuit joined to it.
Origin of gamma rays
Gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom. They are the part of the electromagnetic spectrum whose source is nuclear rather than a change involving the electrons of the atom.
Emission and absorption by atoms

Changes in atoms and the nuclei of atoms can result in electromagnetic waves being generated or absorbed over a wide frequency range. The same kinds of change work in both directions: an atom able to emit a wave of a given frequency can also absorb one.
Ionising radiation

Radiation with enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms, leaving charged particles behind. X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation, and this is why they can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.
Radiation dose

Radiation dose (in sieverts) is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure of the body to the radiation. It is not a count of waves or of decays: it is a measure of risk, and the harm depends on the type of radiation as well as on the size of the dose.
Sievert and millisievert

The two sizes of unit used for radiation dose in this specification are related by 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv). To change a dose in mSv into Sv, divide by 1000; to change a dose in Sv into mSv, multiply by 1000.
Effects of ultraviolet on skin
Ultraviolet waves can cause skin to age prematurely and increase the risk of skin cancer. These are the two effects of ultraviolet on human body tissue named by the specification.
Mutation of genes

A change to a gene inside a cell. X-rays and gamma rays are ionising radiation that can cause the mutation of genes and cancer, so damage from these waves is damage to the material inside cells rather than simple heating of tissue.
Comparing doses from given data

To draw a conclusion about risk from a table of doses, first put every dose into the same unit using 1000 mSv = 1 Sv, then compare the numbers. Only once the units match does a larger number mean a larger risk of harm.

physics-uses-and-applications-of-electro.d: Physics — Uses and applications of electromagnetic waves
terms: Practical application of an electromagnetic wave

A use made of one group of the electromagnetic spectrum. The specification lists radio waves with television and radio; microwaves with satellite communications and cooking food; infrared with electrical heaters, cooking food and infrared cameras; visible light with fibre optic communications; ultraviolet with energy efficient lamps and sun tanning; and X-rays and gamma rays with medical imaging and treatments.
Radio waves – television and radio

Radio waves are the longest-wavelength group of the spectrum and are used to broadcast television and radio programmes. A transmitter converts the signal into radio waves, and an aerial on a house or a receiver picks them up and converts them back.
Microwaves – satellite communications and cooking food

Microwaves have shorter wavelengths than radio waves. They are used to carry signals up to satellites and back down to earth, and in a microwave oven, where they are absorbed by the food and increase its energy store.
Infrared – heaters, cooking and cameras

Infrared is emitted by all objects, and by more the hotter they are. It is used in electrical heaters and grills, where it is absorbed by the surface it falls on, and in infrared cameras, which form an image from the infrared an object emits.
Visible light – fibre optic communications
Visible light is the narrow band of the spectrum the eye detects. In fibre optic communications, information is sent as very rapid pulses of light that travel along a thin glass fibre.
Ultraviolet – energy efficient lamps and sun tanning

Ultraviolet has shorter wavelengths than visible light. It is produced inside an energy efficient (fluorescent) lamp and converted to visible light by the coating on the tube, and it is used in sunbeds and sunlight to tan skin, though it can damage skin cells.
X-rays and gamma rays – medical imaging and treatments

X-rays and gamma rays are the shortest-wavelength groups. They are used to make images of the inside of the body, because bone absorbs them far more than soft tissue does, and in treatment, where a beam is directed at a tumour to destroy its cells.
Absorption and transmission decide the use (HT)

Whether a wave is suitable for an application depends on what absorbs it and what lets it through. Microwaves suit satellite links because the atmosphere transmits them; infrared suits a grill because food absorbs it; X-rays suit imaging because bone absorbs them and flesh does not.
Fluorescent coating (HT)

The layer on the inside of an energy efficient lamp that absorbs the ultraviolet produced in the tube and re-emits the energy as visible light, so the lamp lights the room without releasing ultraviolet into it.

biology-the-development-of-understanding.d: Biology — The development of understanding of genetics and evolution
terms: Evidence for evolution

Evidence for Darwin's theory is now available as it has been shown that characteristics are passed on to offspring in genes. There is further evidence in the fossil record and in the knowledge of how resistance to antibiotics evolves in bacteria. Because of this evidence the theory of evolution by natural selection is now widely accepted, which is the impact these ideas have had on biology.
Fossil
The 'remains' of organisms from millions of years ago, which are found in rocks.
Formation of fossils

Fossils may be formed from parts of organisms that have not decayed because one or more of the conditions needed for decay are absent, when parts of the organism are replaced by minerals as they decay, or as preserved traces of organisms, such as footprints, burrows and rootlet traces.
Gaps in the early fossil record

Many early forms of life were soft-bodied, which means that they have left few traces behind. What traces there were have been mainly destroyed by geological activity. This is why scientists cannot be certain about how life began on Earth.
Evolutionary tree

A diagram, built from evidence such as the fossil record, in which a branch point shows a common ancestor shared by the organisms on the branches above it. Evolutionary trees and other charts, graphs and tables let us learn from fossils how much or how little different organisms have changed as life developed on Earth.
Extinction
Extinctions occur when there are no remaining individuals of a species still alive.
Factors contributing to extinction

A species may become extinct because of changes to the environment over geological time, new predators, new diseases, new more successful competitors, or a single catastrophic event such as a massive volcanic eruption or a collision with an asteroid.
Rapid evolution in bacteria
Bacteria can evolve rapidly because they reproduce at a fast rate.
Antibiotic resistant strain

Mutations of bacterial pathogens produce new strains. Some strains might be resistant to antibiotics, and so are not killed. They survive and reproduce, so the population of the resistant strain rises. The resistant strain will then spread because people are not immune to it and there is no effective treatment.
MRSA
A strain of bacteria which is resistant to antibiotics.
Reducing the development of resistant strains

To reduce the rate of development of antibiotic resistant strains, doctors should not prescribe antibiotics inappropriately, such as treating non-serious or viral infections; patients should complete their course of antibiotics so all bacteria are killed and none survive to mutate and form resistant strains; and the agricultural use of antibiotics should be restricted.
Development of new antibiotics
The development of new antibiotics is costly and slow. It is unlikely to keep up with the emergence of new resistant strains.
Linnaean system
The traditional system of classification, developed by Carl Linnaeus, in which living things are classified into groups depending on their structure and characteristics.
Linnaean groups

The groups Linnaeus classified living things into: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. Kingdom is the largest group and species the smallest, so organisms placed in the same genus share more characteristics than organisms placed only in the same class.
Binomial system
The system used to name organisms, in which an organism is given a two-part name made up of its genus followed by its species, for example Panthera leo.
New models of classification

Classification systems proposed after Linnaeus. As evidence of internal structures became more developed due to improvements in microscopes, and the understanding of biochemical processes progressed, new models of classification were proposed.
Three-domain system

The system developed by Carl Woese, due to evidence available from chemical analysis, in which organisms are divided into Archaea (primitive bacteria usually living in extreme environments), Bacteria (true bacteria) and Eukaryota (which includes protists, fungi, plants and animals).
Evolutionary tree
A method used by scientists to show how they believe organisms are related, drawn using current classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct organisms.
Ecosystem
The interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment.
Habitat
The place where an organism lives. It supplies the conditions and the materials the organism needs from its surroundings in order to survive and reproduce.
Population
All the organisms of one species living in a habitat. A population is the level of organisation between the individual organism and the community.
Community
The populations of all the different species living together in a habitat. Within a community each species depends on the other species living there.
Competition

Organisms of the same or different species competing for the same resource where the supply is limited. Plants in a community or habitat often compete with each other for light and space, and for water and mineral ions from the soil. Animals often compete with each other for food, mates and territory.
Interdependence
Within a community each species depends on other species for food, shelter, pollination, seed dispersal etc. If one species is removed it can affect the whole community.
Stable community
A community where all the species and environmental factors are in balance so that population sizes remain fairly constant.
Abiotic factor

A non-living factor which can affect a community. The abiotic factors are: light intensity; temperature; moisture levels; soil pH and mineral content; wind intensity and direction; carbon dioxide levels for plants; oxygen levels for aquatic animals.
Biotic factor

A living factor which can affect a community. The biotic factors are: availability of food; new predators arriving; new pathogens; one species outcompeting another so the numbers are no longer sufficient to breed.
Adaptation
A feature that an organism has which enables it to survive in the conditions in which it normally lives.
Structural, behavioural and functional adaptations

The three types of adaptation. Structural adaptations are features of the organism's body, such as its shape or covering. Behavioural adaptations are things the organism does. Functional adaptations are the ways processes inside the organism's body work.
Extremophile
An organism that lives in an environment that is very extreme, such as at high temperature, pressure, or salt concentration. Bacteria living in deep sea vents are extremophiles.
Materials required to survive and reproduce

To survive and reproduce, organisms require a supply of materials from their surroundings and from the other living organisms there, for example light, water and mineral ions for a plant, and food from other organisms for an animal.

chemistry-carbon-compounds-as-fuels-and-.d: Chemistry — Carbon compounds as fuels and feedstock
terms: Crude oil
A finite resource found in rocks; the remains of an ancient biomass consisting mainly of plankton that was buried in mud.
Finite resource
A resource that is being used up far faster than it is formed, so the supply will eventually run out.
Biomass
Material that was once living. The biomass that formed crude oil consisted mainly of plankton.
Mixture
Two or more substances that are not chemically joined together. Crude oil is a mixture of a very large number of compounds.
Hydrocarbon
A molecule made up of hydrogen and carbon atoms only.
Alkane
The homologous series that most of the hydrocarbons in crude oil belong to, with the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
Homologous series
A family of similar compounds that share a general formula, such as the alkanes.
General formula
A formula that gives the number of each kind of atom in terms of n. For alkanes it is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
Molecular formula
A formula such as C₂H₆ that gives the number of atoms of each element in one molecule.
Displayed formula
A drawing that shows every atom in a molecule and the covalent bonds between them.
Methane
The first alkane, CH₄; one carbon atom joined to four hydrogen atoms.
Ethane
The second alkane, C₂H₆; two carbon atoms joined to each other and to six hydrogen atoms.
Propane
The third alkane, C₃H₈.
Butane
The fourth alkane, C₄H₁₀.
Fraction
A part of crude oil separated by fractional distillation, containing molecules with a similar number of carbon atoms.
Fractional distillation
Separating the hydrocarbons in crude oil into fractions by evaporating the oil and condensing each fraction at a different temperature.
Evaporation
Turning a liquid into a vapour. The heated crude oil evaporates before it enters the fractionating column.
Condensation
Turning a vapour back into a liquid. Each fraction condenses where the column has cooled to its boiling point.
Feedstock
A raw material fed into a chemical process. Crude oil fractions are used as feedstock for the petrochemical industry.
Petrochemical industry
The industry that turns crude oil fractions into useful materials such as solvents, lubricants, polymers and detergents.
Boiling point
The temperature at which a liquid boils. For hydrocarbons it increases as the molecules get larger.
Viscosity
How thick a liquid is and how easily it flows. Hydrocarbons become more viscous as the molecules get larger.
Flammability
How easily a substance catches fire. Hydrocarbons become less flammable as the molecules get larger.
Combustion
Burning a fuel in oxygen, which releases energy.
Complete combustion
Burning a hydrocarbon in plenty of oxygen so that the only products are carbon dioxide and water.
Oxidation
Gain of oxygen. During combustion both the carbon and the hydrogen in the fuel are oxidised.
Cracking
Breaking down hydrocarbons to produce smaller, more useful molecules.
Catalytic cracking
Cracking in which hydrocarbon vapour is passed over a hot catalyst.
Steam cracking
Cracking in which hydrocarbon vapour is mixed with steam and heated to a very high temperature.
Alkene
A type of hydrocarbon produced by cracking. Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes.
Bromine water test
Adding bromine water to a hydrocarbon. An alkene turns the orange bromine water colourless; an alkane does not.
Polymer
A very long molecule made by joining many small molecules together. Alkenes are used to produce polymers.

physics-permanent-and-induced-magnetism-.d: Physics — Permanent and induced magnetism, magnetic forces and fields
terms: Pole of a magnet
A pole is a place on a magnet where the magnetic forces are strongest. A bar magnet has two: a north (seeking) pole and a south (seeking) pole, one at each end.
Like and unlike poles
Like poles are two poles of the same kind (N and N, or S and S) and they repel each other. Unlike poles are one north and one south, and they attract each other.
Non-contact force
A force that acts between two objects that are not touching. Attraction and repulsion between two magnetic poles are examples of non-contact force.
Permanent magnet
A magnet that produces its own magnetic field. It keeps that field whether or not any other magnet is nearby, and it has a fixed north pole and south pole.
Induced magnet

A material that becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field. Induced magnetism always causes a force of attraction, and when the material is removed from the field it loses most or all of its magnetism quickly.
Magnetic field
The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material.
Magnetic material
A material on which a magnet exerts a force of attraction. The specification names iron, steel, cobalt and nickel.
Field strength and distance
The strength of the magnetic field depends on the distance from the magnet: it is strongest at the poles and gets weaker as the distance from the magnet increases.
Direction of a magnetic field
The direction of the magnetic field at any point is the direction of the force that would act on another north pole placed at that point.
Magnetic field line

A line used to represent a magnetic field. Its direction is from the north (seeking) pole of a magnet to the south (seeking) pole of the magnet, and lines drawn closer together represent a stronger field.
Magnetic compass
An instrument containing a small bar magnet that is free to turn. The needle lines up with, and points in the direction of, the magnetic field it sits in.
Earth's magnetic field
The Earth has a magnetic field, and a compass needle placed away from other magnets points in the direction of the Earth's magnetic field.
Plotting a field pattern

A method of finding a field pattern: place a compass near the magnet, mark a dot at each end of the needle, move the compass so its tail sits on the previous head dot, repeat, then join the dots into a line and add an arrow.
Evidence for a magnetic core

A compass points the same way anywhere on the Earth's surface with no magnet nearby. The field must therefore be produced by the Earth itself, which is evidence that the core of the Earth must be magnetic.
Producer

The organism at the start of a food chain, which synthesises molecules. It is usually a green plant or alga which makes glucose by photosynthesis. Photosynthetic organisms are the producers of biomass for life on Earth.
Food chain

A way of representing feeding relationships within a community. All food chains begin with a producer, which is eaten by a primary consumer, which in turn may be eaten by secondary consumers and then tertiary consumers.
Primary consumer
An organism that eats producers. Primary consumers may in turn be eaten by secondary consumers.
Secondary consumer
An organism that eats primary consumers. Secondary consumers may in turn be eaten by tertiary consumers.
Predator and prey
Consumers that kill and eat other animals are predators, and those eaten are prey. In a stable community the numbers of predators and prey rise and fall in cycles.
Quadrat

A square frame of known area placed on the ground, used by ecologists to determine the abundance of a species by counting the organisms inside it. Quadrats are placed at random positions so that the sample represents the whole area.
Transect
A line marked across a habitat, along which quadrats are placed at intervals. Transects are used by ecologists to determine how the distribution of a species changes across an ecosystem.
Arithmetic mean

The total of all the readings divided by the number of readings, used to summarise the abundance of a species from repeated quadrat counts. It differs from the median, which is the middle value when the readings are put in order, and the mode, which is the most common value.
Abiotic and biotic components
The non-living (abiotic) and living (biotic) parts of an ecosystem. Many different materials cycle through the abiotic and biotic components of an ecosystem.
Recycling of materials
All materials in the living world are recycled to provide the building blocks for future organisms, rather than being used once and lost.
Carbon cycle
The cycle that returns carbon from organisms to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, to be used by plants in photosynthesis.
Water cycle
The cycle that provides fresh water for plants and animals on land before draining into the seas. Water is continuously evaporated and precipitated.
Magnetic effect of a current

Whenever a current flows in a conducting wire, a magnetic field is produced in the space around the wire. The field exists only while the current flows: switch the current off and the field disappears.
Field pattern around a straight wire

The field lines around a long straight current-carrying wire are concentric circles lying in a plane at right angles to the wire and centred on it. The circles are drawn close together near the wire and further apart further away, showing that the field is strongest close to the wire.
Factors affecting the field around a wire

The strength of the magnetic field around a wire depends on two things: the current through the wire, and the distance from the wire. A larger current gives a stronger field; moving further from the wire gives a weaker field.
Direction of the field around a wire

The direction of the circular field lines is shown by arrowheads and is given by the right-hand grip rule: point the right thumb along the conventional current and the curled fingers give the direction of the field lines. Reversing the current reverses every arrow.
Solenoid

A solenoid is a wire wound into a long coil of many turns. Shaping the wire this way increases the strength of the magnetic field produced by a given current, because the field of each turn adds to the field of its neighbours.
Field inside a solenoid

Inside a current-carrying solenoid the magnetic field is strong and uniform: the same strength and direction everywhere inside the coil. It is drawn as straight, evenly spaced, parallel lines running along the axis of the coil.
Field outside a solenoid

Outside the coil the field spreads out and has a similar shape to the field of a bar magnet, with one end of the solenoid behaving as a north pole and the other as a south pole. The lines outside run from the north end round to the south end, and every line is a closed loop that continues through the inside of the coil.
Iron core

A core of iron placed inside a solenoid is magnetised by the field of the coil and greatly increases the strength of the magnetic field. Iron is used because it loses almost all of its magnetism as soon as the current is switched off.
Electromagnet
An electromagnet is a solenoid with an iron core. Its magnetic field can be switched on and off with the current, and its strength can be changed by changing the current or the number of turns.
Demonstrating the magnetic effect

The magnetic effect of a current is demonstrated by placing plotting compasses, or scattering iron filings, near a wire and switching the current on: the compasses swing round to lie end to end along circles around the wire, and swing back to north when the current is switched off.
Increasing the magnetic effect

The magnetic effect of a current can be increased by increasing the current, by winding the wire into a solenoid with more turns so that the fields of the turns add together, and by adding an iron core.
Electromagnetic relay

In a relay a small current in a coil magnetises an iron core, which attracts a pivoted iron armature; the armature closes contacts in a second, separate circuit. A small current can therefore switch on a much larger one, and the two circuits stay electrically isolated from each other.
Electric bell

In an electric bell the current passes through an electromagnet that attracts an iron armature carrying a hammer; as the armature moves it breaks the circuit, the electromagnet switches off, a spring pulls the armature back and the circuit is remade, so the hammer strikes repeatedly.
Motor effect
When a conductor carrying a current is placed in a magnetic field, the magnet producing the field and the conductor exert a force on each other. This is called the motor effect.
Fleming's left-hand rule

Hold the thumb, first finger and second finger of the left hand at right angles to one another. The First finger points along the Field, the seCond finger along the Current, and the thuMb then gives the direction of the force, that is the Motion of the conductor.
Factors affecting the size of the force
The size of the force on a conductor in a magnetic field depends on the magnetic flux density of the field, the current through the conductor, and the length of conductor that is inside the field.
Magnetic flux density
Magnetic flux density, symbol B, is the measure of the strength of a magnetic field used in this equation. It is measured in tesla, T, and a stronger magnet gives a larger flux density.
Force on a conductor equation
For a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field and carrying a current: force = magnetic flux density × current × length, written in symbols as F = B I l.
Tesla
The tesla, T, is the unit of magnetic flux density. A flux density of 1 T gives a force of 1 N on each metre of a conductor carrying a current of 1 A at right angles to the field.
Symbols and units in F = B I l

Force, F, in newtons, N; magnetic flux density, B, in tesla, T; current, I, in amperes, A (amp is acceptable for ampere); length, l, in metres, m. Values must be substituted in these units, so a length given in centimetres has to be converted to metres first.
Turning effect on a coil

A coil of wire carrying a current in a magnetic field tends to rotate, because the forces on its two opposite sides act in opposite directions and so turn the coil about its axle. This is the basis of an electric motor.
Split-ring commutator

The split-ring commutator reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn, just as the coil passes the vertical. The forces on the two sides therefore swap over at the right moment, and the coil keeps rotating in the same direction instead of stopping and rocking back.

biology-biodiversity-and-the-effect-of-h.d: Biology — Biodiversity and the effect of human interaction on ecosystems
terms: Biodiversity
The variety of all the different species of organisms on earth, or within an ecosystem.
Biodiversity and the stability of ecosystems
A great biodiversity ensures the stability of ecosystems by reducing the dependence of one species on another for food, shelter and the maintenance of the physical environment.
Maintaining biodiversity

The future of the human species on Earth relies on us maintaining a good level of biodiversity. Many human activities are reducing biodiversity and only recently have measures been taken to try to stop this reduction.
Human population growth and standard of living

Rapid growth in the human population and an increase in the standard of living mean that increasingly more resources are used and more waste is produced. Unless waste and chemical materials are properly handled, more pollution will be caused.
Pollution

Pollution can occur in water, from sewage, fertiliser or toxic chemicals; in air, from smoke and acidic gases; and on land, from landfill and from toxic chemicals. Pollution kills plants and animals which can reduce biodiversity.
Human use of land
Humans reduce the amount of land available for other animals and plants by building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste.
Destruction of peat bogs

The destruction of peat bogs, and other areas of peat to produce garden compost, reduces the area of this habitat and thus the variety of different plant, animal and microorganism species that live there (biodiversity).
Carbon dioxide from peat
The decay or burning of the peat releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
Global warming
Levels of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere are increasing, and contribute to 'global warming'.
Programmes to protect ecosystems and biodiversity

Scientists and concerned citizens have put in place programmes to reduce the negative effects of humans on ecosystems and biodiversity. These include: breeding programmes for endangered species; protection and regeneration of rare habitats; reintroduction of field margins and hedgerows in agricultural areas where farmers grow only one type of crop; reduction of deforestation and carbon dioxide emissions by some governments; recycling resources rather than dumping waste in landfill.
Pure substance (chemical meaning)
In chemistry, a pure substance is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance. Purity is a statement about what is in the sample, not about how clean, clear or natural it looks.
Mixture

Two or more elements or compounds that are not chemically combined. The substances keep their own properties, which is why a mixture melts and boils over a range of temperatures rather than at one temperature.
Pure (everyday meaning)

In everyday language a pure substance is one that has had nothing added to it, so it is unadulterated and in its natural state, eg pure milk. Such a substance is almost always a mixture in the chemical sense.
Melting point
The specific temperature at which a pure element or compound changes from solid to liquid. A pure substance melts sharply at that one temperature rather than over a range.
Boiling point
The specific temperature at which a pure element or compound changes from liquid to gas. A pure liquid boils steadily at that one temperature while it all turns to gas.
Using melting and boiling data to test purity

Compare the measured value with the data book value for the pure substance, and look at whether the change happens at one temperature or over a range. An impurity lowers a melting point and raises a boiling point, and in both cases spreads the change over a range.
Formulation
A mixture that has been designed as a useful product. Many products are complex mixtures in which each chemical has a particular purpose.
Measured quantities in a formulation

Formulations are made by mixing the components in carefully measured quantities to ensure that the product has the required properties. Change the proportions and the product no longer does its job properly.
Examples of formulations
Formulations include fuels, cleaning agents, paints, medicines, alloys, fertilisers and foods. Each is a mixture, so a formulation is never a pure substance.
Chromatography
A technique that can be used to separate mixtures and can give information to help identify substances. It involves a stationary phase and a mobile phase.
Stationary phase
The phase that does not move. In paper chromatography the paper is the stationary phase, and a substance attracted strongly to it is held back near the origin.
Mobile phase
The phase that moves. In paper chromatography the solvent is the mobile phase, and it carries dissolved substances up the paper as it rises.
Distribution between the phases

Separation depends on the distribution of substances between the phases. A substance more attracted to the solvent than to the paper spends more time moving and travels further; a substance held more strongly by the paper travels less far.
Rf value

The ratio of the distance moved by a compound (centre of spot from origin) to the distance moved by the solvent: R_f= (distance moved by substance) / (distance moved by solvent). It is a ratio of two distances, so it has no units and is always less than 1.
Identifying compounds from Rf values

Different compounds have different Rf values in different solvents, which can be used to help identify the compounds. The compounds in a mixture may separate into different spots depending on the solvent, but a pure compound will produce a single spot in all solvents.
Origin (baseline)
The pencil line on which the samples are spotted. The distance moved by a compound is measured from this line to the centre of its spot.
Solvent front
The furthest point the solvent reaches up the paper, marked in pencil as soon as the paper is taken out. The distance moved by the solvent is measured from the origin to this line.
Significant figures in an Rf value

An answer is given to an appropriate number of significant figures, which means no more than the measurements it came from. Distances read to two significant figures give an Rf value quoted to two significant figures.
Required practical 6

Investigate how paper chromatography can be used to separate and tell the difference between coloured substances, calculating Rf values. The start line is drawn in pencil and the solvent in the container starts below that line.
test for hydrogen
A burning splint is held at the open end of a test tube of the gas; hydrogen burns rapidly with a pop sound.
burning splint
A wooden splint that has been lit so it carries a flame; it is held at the open end of the test tube in the hydrogen test.
pop sound
The short, sharp squeak heard as hydrogen burns rapidly at the mouth of the test tube; it is the positive result for hydrogen.
test for oxygen
A glowing splint is inserted into a test tube of the gas; the splint relights in oxygen.
glowing splint
A splint that has been lit and then blown out, so the tip is still glowing red hot but carries no flame.
relight
The glowing tip of the splint bursts back into flame when it is inserted into oxygen; this is the positive result for oxygen.
limewater
An aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide, used as the test reagent for carbon dioxide.
test for carbon dioxide
Carbon dioxide is shaken with or bubbled through limewater; the limewater turns milky (cloudy).
milky (cloudy)
The white, opaque appearance limewater takes on when carbon dioxide is passed through it; it is the positive result for carbon dioxide.
test for chlorine
Damp litmus paper is put into the chlorine gas; the litmus paper is bleached and turns white.
damp litmus paper
Litmus paper moistened with water before it is put into the gas; the chlorine test uses damp, not dry, litmus paper.
bleached
The colour of the litmus paper is removed so that the paper turns white; this is the positive result for chlorine.
Key idea in physics

One of a small number of ideas used to describe the complex and diverse phenomena of the natural and man-made world. A key idea is a way of thinking that recurs across the whole subject rather than a detail belonging to one topic.
Universal application

The property of the key ideas that they apply everywhere in the subject content rather than in one topic. Because they are embedded throughout the content, they underpin the assessment and are assessed across all papers.
Model

A simplified representation of a system or process, used to describe, explain and predict behaviour. A model is judged by how well it explains and predicts, not by whether it contains every detail of the real thing.
Particle model of matter
A model in which matter is treated as a large number of small particles, with the arrangement and motion of those particles used to explain the properties of solids, liquids and gases.
Wave model

A model in which a phenomenon is treated as a wave, so that quantities such as wavelength, frequency and amplitude can be used. Light is modelled as a transverse wave and sound as a longitudinal wave.
Cause and effect
